en: Preface to the Collected Treatises on Birth and Non-Birth in the Pure Land To speak with precision, the Pure Land is neither birth nor non-birth. Why is this?

The Pure Land is but another name for the nature of the mind. It is fundamentally free from delusion and defilement; it is merely designated as "pure" by convention. It is that upon which sentient beings rely.
It is provisionally named "earth. Since it is one's own mind, both "arising" and "non-arising" become mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
What is now called "arising" refers to the Great Compassionate Father, who, out of deep concern for his children, acts at the gateway of the second door to extract suffering and bestow happiness;

this is the meaning of the gate of arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). Furthermore, what is called "non-arising" refers to the ancient spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) acting for [the sake of beings]...
The depth of the Buddha’s Dharma is profound. Relying upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he administers medicine according to the illness;

this is the purport of the True Suchness Gate (*tathatā-mukha*). These two gates are but the one mind, which speaks of both arising and non-arising. Nevertheless, the one mind fully encompasses these two gates.
It does not hinder arising or non-arising. For this reason, the ancients called it "leaning against the gate and waiting for one's son.
If you can understand it in this way, you will be able to perfectly transcend the four propositions and perfectly encompass them; it is absolute, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable.
Spontaneously transcending emotion and departing from views, you will avoid the reproach of being like a vine clinging to a tree, and you will not touch upon the mass of fire.

This is a lament. Alas! At such a time as this, it is precisely the late autumn of the Dharma Garden and the deep winter of the Ocean of Monks. Wherever one looks in the frosty forest, there are only "lion-insects" (parasites);

throughout the icy sea, there are nothing but "crane-of-the-rainy-season" (pretenders). Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to appear once more, there would be no gate through which they could be seen.
What kind of people are we that we dare to wag our tongues and move our lips? We do so only to maintain the lineage and sustain the tradition.
It was simply that I could not help myself. He asked, "Who are you? Without even weighing your own capacity, how dare you venture to compose a commentary?
He replied, "I am no one in particular. In truth, I too do not dare to compose a commentary.

This book is merely a collection of some leftover broth and stale rice gathered during the intervals of my illness; it is intended only for my own consumption. I did not expect that those looking on would not find it distasteful."

Regarding those who are sour and stinking, I have pressed them closely and taken [their writings] from them; this was not a matter of failing to exercise self-restraint. However, these are leftovers from their meals.
Although they cannot satisfy the mouths of others, they will provide some small benefit to us who criticize those who starve.

As for the title "Collected Works" (*Huìjí*), it refers to the single section on explaining titles (*shìtí*). All of it was penned by Master Chè; had I not collected it, I fear it might be lost to posterity.
The writings contained herein have all drawn upon the essential meanings of the Tiantai school. Had they not been synthesized, I fear there might have been omissions in detail.
Now, having integrated and compiled them, I have given it this title.

This commentary is divided into three major sections: first, the general presentation of the title of the treatise; second, the request for [divine] assistance and the statement of the intent.
The treatise is established through three topical divisions. The first [division] further has two parts: first, the title of the treatise; second, the author of the treatise.

The first [of these] further has three parts: first, an explanation of the "Pure Land"; second, an explanation of "birth" and "non-birth"; third, an explanation of the word "treatise" (*śāstra*). First, the explanation of the Pure Land further has four parts.

First, the four lands are explained; second, their origins are described; third, their fundamental purpose is clarified; fourth, their superior benefits are revealed. The first section [on the names and meanings] further has three parts: first, the names and meanings of the four lands are explained; second, the defiled and pure aspects of the four lands are explained; third, the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the four lands are explained. The first of these [the names] further has two parts: first, the enumeration of the names; second, the analysis of their meanings. Now, the first [the enumeration of the names]: 1. The Land of Constantly Quiescent Light and Adornments 2. The Land of Eternally Tranquil Light and Virtues 3. The Land of Exquisite Adornment and Unobstructed Freedom 4. The Land of Peaceful Sustenance and Joyful Transformation The first [the Land of Constantly Quiescent Light and Adornments] is so named because it is eternally free from all afflictions and obstacles, and its physical environment and sentient beings are adorned with immeasurable marks and characteristics. The second [the Land of Eternally Tranquil Light and Virtues] is so named because its physical environment and sentient beings are adorned with immeasurable virtues of light and tranquility. The third [the Land of Exquisite Adornment and Unobstructed Freedom] is so named because its physical environment and sentient beings are adorned with immeasurable exquisite adornments and possess unimpeded freedom. The fourth [the Land of Peaceful Sustenance and Joyful Transformation] is so named because its physical environment and sentient beings are sustained by peaceful provisions and experience joyful transformations. Next, the analysis of the meanings. First, the Land of Constantly Quiescent Light and Adornments: "Constantly quiescent" means that all afflictions and obstacles have forever ceased. "Light" refers to the illumination of wisdom. "Adornments" refers to the embellishments of the physical environment and sentient beings. Second, the Land of Eternally Tranquil Light and Virtues: "Eternally tranquil" means that all disturbances have forever subsided. "Light" refers to the radiance of the Dharma-realm. "Virtues" refers to the qualities of the physical environment and sentient beings. Third, the Land of Exquisite Adornment and Unobstructed Freedom: "Exquisite adornment" refers to the magnificent array of the physical environment and sentient beings. "Unobstructed freedom" refers to the mastery over the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. Fourth, the Land of Peaceful Sustenance and Joyful Transformation: "Peaceful sustenance" refers to the provision of the necessities for life through the power of the Buddha’s vows. "Joyful transformation" refers to the spontaneous manifestation of various forms according to the inclinations of sentient beings. "Name" refers to the names of the four lands (*bhūmi*). As for the four lands, they are the realms upon which the sentient beings of the ten dharma-realms rely.
Although these lands are infinite, they are briefly subsumed into four: first, the land of eternal quiescent light; second, the land of true retribution without obstruction;
third, the land of expedient means with remainder; and fourth, the land of common residence for ordinary beings and sages. By means of these four lands, the ten [realms] are subsumed.
Regarding the realms: Quiescent Radiance is the Buddha-land; True Reward is the land of the Bodhisattvas; Expedient Means is the land of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
and Shared Residence is the land of the six classes of ordinary beings.

II. Explaining the Meanings, which again has four parts. First is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*), up to the fourth, the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages (*pṛthagjana-ārya-saha-vāsa-kṣetra*).
Now, for the first:

The Land of Constant Quiescent Light is that wherein all Buddhas dwell; it is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa-rahasya-kośa*). It is distinguished into the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding the two virtues: as for the "intrinsic virtue" (*xingde*), it refers to the fundamental nature of the mind possessed by all sentient beings.

The *Profound Meaning of the Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "Permanence is the Dharma-body; tranquility is liberation; and radiance is prajñā. Furthermore, all three virtues are permanent because their nature does not undergo change;
all three virtues are tranquil because they are free from worldly afflictions; and all three virtues are radiant because they are supremely luminous and pure.
These three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal; they are called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*).

This is precisely what is referred to in the subsequent sections of the treatise as the essence of nature (*xingti*), the magnitude of nature (*xingliang*), and the inherent possession of nature (*xingju*). The essence of nature is the inherently possessed virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the magnitude of nature is the inherently possessed virtue of Prajñā;
and the inherent possession of nature is the inherently possessed virtue of Liberation (*vimukti*). These are also the Three Truths (*tisatyāni*): the permanent is the Middle Way.
The "stillness" is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the "light" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since they are one yet discussed as three, they are not sequential;

since they are three yet discussed as one, they are not horizontal. Being neither sequential nor horizontal, it is inconceivable; therefore, it is called the "Secret Treasury. This is the virtue of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
As for the virtue of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), the subsequent text states: "Those who cultivate it do so by illuminating and realizing in accordance with its nature."

That is to say: by practicing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one destroys the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); this accords with the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and accomplishes the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*).

By practicing the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*), one destroys the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust; this accords with the nature of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and accomplishes the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). By practicing the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*), one destroys ignorance (*avidyā*);

this accords with the nature of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) and accomplishes the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*). When nature and practice are discussed in conjunction, this is the sphere of activity of the pure Dharma-body (*viśuddha-dharmakāya*).

Regarding "abiding": when defined in terms of the principle of inherent nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), it is called "land" (*kṣetra*); when defined in terms of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), it is called "body" (*kāya*).

Body and land are of one suchness; they do not possess two distinct characteristics. There is no sense here of separate or individual differentiation, yet they actually pervade throughout the various differentiated realms, for apart from this [oneness], there is no other locus where those differentiated realms can be established.
II. The Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction.
Regarding the "Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction": it accords with the true mark (*dharmatā*) and is the genuine fruit of retribution; therefore, it is called "true reward."
Matter and mind are sovereign, and the dust-motes and lands mutually contain one another; hence it is called "unobstructed.
This land is where the great beings of the forty-first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) and those above the stages of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) dwell and travel.

The body can manifest the land, and the land likewise manifests the body, without violating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Its supreme and wondrous adornments are fully as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The Dharma-realm is peaceful.

This is the Established Sea (*sthita-sāgara*). It is also called the Land of Partial Realization of the Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prasānta-ābhāsvara-kṣetra*), for it is the dwelling place of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
○ Third, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-avaśeṣa-bhūmi*).
Regarding the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder: outside the three realms (*tridhātu*) there is a pure land where the holy ones of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) cultivate skillful means.

It is the dwelling place where expedient means (*upāya*) operate; hence it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Because one has exhausted only the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), yet has not eliminated the distinct delusions (*viśeṣa-avidyā*);

and because one has merely transcended the stage of segmented death (*paricchinna-maraṇa*), yet has not yet avoided the death of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*); it is therefore called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). This refers to nine types of persons born in this land:

two from the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) teaching—the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha—and three from the Shared (*Sādhāraṇa*) teaching—the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the [Bodhisattva of] the sixth [stage].
From the stage of the Ground upward, there are three persons according to the Separate Teaching: those of the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, and the Ten Dedications;

and one person according to the Perfect Teaching: namely, those of the Ten Faiths. These nine persons cultivate only the contemplation of emptiness and sever the universal delusions of views and thoughts.

Although those of the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] cultivate the provisional and the middle, they have not yet shattered ignorance nor realized the truth; therefore, it is called the "expedient" stage.
It is also named the Land of Real Reward, for it is the land of real reward for the noble ones of the Three Vehicles.
○ Fourth, the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages.

Regarding the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages: it is originally that which is summoned and manifested by the tainted wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable karmas of ordinary beings;
yet sages also dwell therein together. Hence, it is called the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages. First...
First, the clarification of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); next, the clarification of noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding ordinary beings, this refers to the nine stages within the three realms.

The three realms refer to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The nine stages refer to: first, the stage of mixed habitation with the five destinies;

second, the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion; third, the stage of joy and bliss born of meditative concentration; fourth, the stage of sublime bliss free from joy; fifth, the stage of equanimity and mindfulness...
The Pure Grounds: 1. The Ground of Infinite Space; 2. The Ground of Infinite Consciousness; 3. The Ground of Nothingness; 4.
The Ground of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. Regarding the first [of the five], the "Mixture of the Five Destinies":

this refers to the interior of the Desire Realm, where the three miserable paths, the human realm, and the six classes of desire-realm devas dwell together; hence it is called the "Mixture of the Five Destinies. Second, the "Separation from Birth" (viveka).
Regarding "joy and bliss": these refer to the three heavens of the first dhyāna—namely, the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā heavens.

Having already become detached from the five desires, one attains the five factors of the first dhyāna: namely, vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and cittaikāgratā (one-pointedness of mind).

Therefore, it is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion. Regarding "joy and bliss born of concentration": these refer to the three heavens of the second dhyāna—namely, the Parīttābha... [and so forth].
The Heaven of the Gods (*Deva*), the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*), and the Heaven of Radiant Sound (*Ābhāsvara*).

These three heavens, having further abandoned the two factors of initial and sustained application (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the first dhyāna, attain the four factors of inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*); therefore, they are called the stage of "joy and bliss born of meditative concentration" (*samādhija-prītisukha-bhūmi*).

Fourth, the stage of "sublime bliss free from joy" refers to the three heavens of the third dhyāna: the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*), the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*), and [the Heaven of Ultimate Purity].

The Heaven of the Gods (*deva*), the Heaven of Utmost Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*). These three heavens further abandon the factor of joy (*prīti*) from the second dhyāna and attain the five factors of the third dhyāna:
equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*); therefore, they are called the "ground of sublime bliss free from joy.

Regarding the "five purities of equanimity and mindfulness," this refers to the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna: the Heaven of Merit-Born (*puṇyaprasava*), the Heaven of Merit-Love (*bṛhatphala*), and the Heaven of Vast Results (*abṛha*)—these three... [and so forth].

These are the heavens of ordinary worldlings; the heaven of non-conception (the heavens of external paths); the Heaven Free from Affliction; the Heaven Free from Heat; the Heaven of Good Vision; and the Heaven of Good Manifestation.
The Akaniṣṭha Heaven (these are the five Anāgāmin heavens, the abodes of noble ones who have attained the third fruit).

These nine heavens further abandon the factors of pleasure from the third dhyāna and attain the four factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*), and neither-pain-nor-pleasure; therefore, they are called the "Ground of Pure Equanimity and Mindfulness.
The four levels above these are named the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), so called because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) constitutes their realm.

Regarding the stage of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*): the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "If, within a mind of equanimity, one achieves the relinquishing of aversion and perceives the body as an obstruction, then by dissolving that obstruction one enters into space; such a class of beings is called the 'Sphere of Space.

Regarding the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*): once all obstructions have been dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation, and therein only the *ālayavijñāna* remains."
The entire manas is half-subtle; such a class [of beings] is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). As for the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*):
since both emptiness and form have vanished and the consciousness-mind has completely ceased, the ten directions are tranquil and there is nowhere to go;

such a class [of beings] is called the Sphere of Nothingness. As for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*): the nature of consciousness is unmoving, because [perception] has been extinguished.
Through exhaustive investigation within the inexhaustible, one proclaims the full realization of nature; it is as if existing yet not existing, as if exhausted yet not exhausted.

This category is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). These four stages are all devoid of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); therefore, they are called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
They are also known as the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), namely: the four continents, the four evil destinies, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma heavens.

The four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and the *anāgāmin*—all such sentient beings possess outflowing causes and effects (*sāsrava-hetu-phala*).

Therefore, they are called the "twenty-five states of existence" (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). This clarifies the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)... [below, the holy one is clarified]. There are two kinds of holy ones:

namely, the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*). The real refers to the four fruits of the *Śrāvaka* vehicle, the six stages of the *Pratyekabuddha*, the ten abodes of the *Vaipulya* (Distinct) vehicle, and the ten [stages] of the Perfect [Vehicle].
Regarding "real": although the pervasive delusions have been severed, the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) still remains; therefore, they are called "real sages. Regarding "expedient":

this refers to these sages who, whether residing in the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), the Land of True Retribution (*bhūtavipāka*), or the Land of Expedient Means (*upāyabhūmi*), manifest out of the power of their great compassionate vows to take pity upon sentient beings.
He manifests birth in this realm not because he is dragged there by karma, but because these two kinds of sages dwell together with ordinary beings;

therefore, it is called the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages. Question: Within the people of the Land of Common Dwelling, there are those who are provisional and those who are real. Are there also provisional and real beings in the three higher lands? Answer:
In the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*), there are two who are provisional and one who is real. This is so if one proceeds from the Land of Common Dwelling toward the severing of delusions.
Birth. As with the nine types of people mentioned previously, these are collectively termed the "one reality.

If viewed from the perspective of the true recompense of the Land of Tranquil Light, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest as dwelling in the realm of expedient means in order to entice those of fixed nature among the two vehicles and bodhisattvas prior to the stages, leading them to enter the correct position.

These are called the two provisional [aspects]. Within the land of true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*), there is one provisional and one real; the forty-one stages are collectively termed the "one real.
The Dharma-Buddha of wondrous enlightenment manifests the marks of the reward-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), which is termed the "provisional.

Within the land of tranquil light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*), there is only the real and no provisional, because it is the place where all Buddhas dwell and roam. This concludes the initial clarification of the names and meanings of the four lands.

II. Clarifying the Defilement and Purity of the Four Lands. Regarding the defilement and purity of the four lands, the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states: "The lightness and heaviness of the five turbidities distinguish the purity and impurity of the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka*). The methods of 'substantiality' and 'analysis,' as well as 'skillfulness' and 'clumsiness,' distinguish the purity and impurity of the Land of Shared [Result]. If one enters suddenly and directly, the distinction between the purity and impurity of the Land of True Reward (*bhūtakoṭi-vipāka*) corresponds to the stages of partial realization and ultimate perfection. Regarding "lightness and heaviness of purity and defilement," the *Miaozong* commentary explains: The five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
When these five turbidities are light, the resulting co-resident world (*sahā-lokadhātu*) is pure, such as the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) or the World of Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*).
When the five turbidities are heavy, it is defiled, such as the present Sahā World. That is, the Sahā...

The *bhava* (existence) is likewise distinguished by purity and defilement. For instance, in the ordinary stages of the four teachings, all cause the turbidity to be lightened, such that what is induced is entirely pure.

Yet in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), even while turbidity is lightened, it induces the most pure environment and beings (*yi-zen*) within the Shared Residence (*tongju*). Regarding the terms "substantial" (*ti*) and "analytical" (*xi*), as well as "skillful" (*qiao*) and "unskillful" (*zhuo*), there are further distinctions between the pure and the defiled.

"Substantial" refers to the contemplation of emptiness through essence (*ti-kong guan*) in the Common Teaching; "analytical" refers to the contemplation of emptiness through analysis (*xi-kong guan*) in the Tripitaka Teaching. This applies to the Common Teaching.

The wisdom of humans is skillful; when applied to contemplation, it is likewise skillful. One thoroughly realizes that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty in their very essence, without needing to wait for analytical deconstruction before knowing they are empty.
By means of this wisdom of essential emptiness, one severs delusions and realizes the truth. The wisdom of those in the *Hīnayāna* (the "Treasury" school) is clumsy.

If one employs contemplation [in this manner], it is clumsy. One must necessarily analyze the four great elements and the five aggregates before realizing the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
By means of this wisdom of analytical emptiness, one cuts off delusions and realizes the Truth. However, the pure aspects in this land are also vast;

while the analytical contemplation that perceives impurity may belong to the Tripiṭaka [Teaching], the contemplation of essence that perceives purity is not exclusive to those of the Shared Teaching. This applies to the three teachings of the Mahāyāna (Yánmén) in contrast to the three [Hinayāna] teachings.

The *Zangxi* (Analysis of the Treasuries) clarifies both the essence and the phenomena. The "General" [teaching] refers to the essence of mere emptiness; the "Specific" refers to the essence of the sequential [stages];

and the "Perfect" refers to the essence of non-sequential [realization]. When these three types of people are born there, they all perceive pure appearances, yet for those of the Perfect [Teaching], these are most pure.

Regarding the statement that one may enter sequentially or instantaneously into the Pure Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*), the "sequential" refers to the specific teaching’s threefold sequential contemplation, while "instantaneous entry" refers to the Perfect Teaching’s single [contemplation].

The mind consists of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Those of the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagjana*) have dull faculties; they do not understand that [the provisional] is identical with the Middle. Therefore, they first practice the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);

next, they practice the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) to sever the afflictions of the sands of dust (*rajas-kaṇa*); and finally, they practice the contemplation of the Middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) to sever ignorance (*avidyā*). Hence, it is called the "successive three contemplations.

Those of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*) have sharp faculties and thoroughly realize that all phenomena are but the single thought-moment of the mind, and that this single thought-moment is replete [with all dharmas].
It encompasses all phenomena. It is neither one nor many; it is both one and many. It is uninterrupted yet severed; it completely severs the five stages of dwelling [in ignorance].
Therefore, it is called "the three contemplations within a single mind. As for the terms "pure" and "defiled": if we discuss the realization of truth, there is only the one purity.
However, in terms of the path of teaching, the ten stages are distinct and not yet fused; what is experienced therein is the defiled. This refers to partial realization and ultimate realization.

"Ultimately, regarding the pure and defiled aspects of *Sāmbhogakāya* Light (*Jig-kwang*): 'partial realization' (*fen-cheng*) refers to the distinct [vehicle] *miao-jue* (wondrous awakening); 'ultimate' (*jiu-jing*) refers to the perfect *miao-jue*.
As for the partial distinction between the pure and the defiled, both the distinct and the perfect *miao-jue* equally realize *Sāmbhogakāya* Light.

If one discusses the severance of delusions, the distinct *miao-jue* severs only twelve grades of ignorance; thus, it is equivalent to the two practices of the perfect [vehicle] and still belongs to the stage of partial realization. The perfect..."
Regarding the teaching on the severance of delusions, there are forty-two grades; this is termed "ultimate. Therefore, it is called "partial realization of the ultimate.
This refers to the Pure Land of Tranquil Light (Jigō-jō) as both pure and defiled.
[Section] Three: The Three Insights and Four Lands, Horizontal and Vertical.

Regarding the discussion of the four lands in terms of vertical and horizontal progression, this is based on the two types of practitioners: those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings. As for the vertical progression:

one emerges from the Land of Common Dwelling and enters the Land of Expedient Means; emerging from the Land of Expedient Means, one enters the Land of Real Reward; and emerging from the Land of Real Reward, one enters the Land of Tranquil Light.
Since the severing of delusions varies in depth, the abodes likewise differ significantly in their height and status. As for the horizontal progression:

Without shifting from one's current location, what is perceived becomes naturally distinct. Within the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), one transcends horizontally the three higher lands:
when the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are exhausted, one sees the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*);

when the secondary afflictions (*anuśaya*) are exhausted and ignorance (*avidyā*) is partially shattered, one sees the Land of Real Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*), and also gains a partial vision of the Land of Peaceful Light (*nirmāṇa-bhūmi*). When ignorance is completely exhausted, one clearly perceives the Land of Peaceful Light.
In the land of skillful means (*upāya-kṣetra*), one transcends horizontally the upper two lands—namely, the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*) and the Land of Quiescent Light (*śānta-prabhāsa*).

In the Land of True Reward, one transcends horizontally one land—namely, the Land of Quiescent Light. In the Land of Quiescent Light, there is nothing further to transcend, nor is there horizontal or vertical progression.

Furthermore, with respect to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the noble ones of the Three Vehicles, they exercise mastery over horizontal and vertical progression within their respective lands; such is the Land of Quiescent Light.

They are able to manifest the three lower lands for the sake of sentient beings: the Land of Real Reward can manifest the two lower lands; the Land of Expedient Means can manifest the Land of Common Residence.
Furthermore, the Land of Common Residence can indicate the three upper lands; the Land of Expedient Means can indicate the two upper lands;
and the Land of Real Reward can indicate the Land of Dharma-Nature and Radiance (Jiguang). The initial analysis of the four lands is complete.

II. An Exposition of Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpāda) As for dependent origination: the deluded mind of the present single thought-moment is, in itself, the universal dependent origination of the one Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Master Che said:
"At the very beginning, when delusion arises from the truth, it is called 'the single thought-moment of deluded movement. At the final stage, when one returns from delusion to the truth..."
It is then said that this is "one-thought resonance. This is precisely the state after the arising of delusion and before the return to truth;
what other dharma could exist outside of this one thought? Therefore, when one thought awakens and follows pure conditions, it is the dependent origination of the Buddha-dharmadhātu;
when it is deluded and follows defiled conditions, it is the dependent origination of the nine dharmadhātus. The empty space of the ten directions is this very one [thought].

Contemplate this delusion and obscurity: all lands are the condensation of this single thought; the primary retributions of the four modes of birth arise from the union and separation of the emotional and conceptual within this single thought;
and the secondary retributions of the four elements result from the movement and stillness, or the opposition and compliance, of this single thought.
All phenomena are manifested in reliance upon this thought alone; apart from this thought, no dharma can be found. Trace this single thought back to its source.
This is fundamentally the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It arises from conditions, yet those conditions lack intrinsic nature;

being entirely the Dharma-realm, it thus extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time. Free from faults and transcending all that is non-existent, it is inconceivable.

By its very nature (*dharmatā*), it possesses this majestic power; by its very nature, it possesses this functional efficacy. Now, with this mindfulness, one recollects Amitābha in the Western Quarter.
When a Buddha-seeker aspires to be born in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, at the very moment of mindfulness, the environment and inhabitants of the West are already within one's own mind,
and this mind of mine is already within the environment and inhabitants of the West— like two mirrors reflecting each other’s light.
Their characteristics contain one another and mutually illuminate; this is the aspect of horizontal pervasiveness throughout the ten directions.

If we consider it in terms of vertical exhaustion across the three periods of time, then the moment one recollects the Buddha is the very moment one sees the Buddha, and also the moment one attains Buddhahood. The moment one seeks birth [in the Pure Land] is the very moment of rebirth there.

This is precisely the moment of delivering sentient beings; the three periods of time are simultaneous, with no sequence of before or after. Like the light of pearls in Indra’s net, it is difficult to equate with the whole;
like the dream-events of the "South Branch" (Nanke), it briefly resembles a single glimpse of the pattern. This principle is most difficult to awaken to, yet easiest to believe.
If one can simply accept it directly, one will ultimately enjoy its full benefit throughout one's entire being. This may be called the completion of one's studies in the Way.
What was to be done has been accomplished. Should you be unable to do so, you should simply observe as you please and make use of things according to your capacity.
The exposition of the dependent origination is concluded.

III. Clarifying the Essential Principle. This also has four parts: first, directly demonstrating that all is mind-only; second, further clarifying the myriad dharmas; third, cutting off... [text ends]

Awaiting the perfect fusion. Fourth, transcending emotion and departing from views. The first [section] is further divided into four parts: first, establishing "Mind-Only" by means of the three measures (pramāṇa), such as direct perception;

second, clarifying the complete manifestation through the two gates of phenomena and principle; third, discerning the true and the false by means of the identity and difference between name and essence;
fourth, resolving and pointing out the fundamental existence that is manifest before us. Now...

First, regarding the "tenet" (zong): it refers to the fundamental tenet. Regarding the "purport" (zhi): it means the underlying intent. One must understand that the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" takes "mind-only" as its tenet.

This meaning of mind-only must be established with certainty by means of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). These three types of valid cognition are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and... [scriptural authority].
*Pramāṇa*. This refers to the authority of the sacred word (*āptavacana-pramāṇa*). *Pratyakṣa-pramāṇa* refers to the direct realization of that principle.

For example, when the Great Master Kumārajīva accompanied his mother to a temple and saw the Buddha’s alms bowl, he joyfully placed it upon the crown of his head. Shortly thereafter, he thought to himself: "I am still very young."
"The Buddha’s bowl is extremely heavy; how can I possibly carry it on my head? As this thought just arose, he suddenly let out a cry and set the bowl down.
Thereupon, he realized that all phenomena are but mind. The Dharma Master Weixiao of Goryeo came to this land to study; one night he stayed among the graves.
He was extremely thirsty. Beneath the bright moon, he saw a pool of clear water; he cupped it in his hands and drank, finding it exceptionally fragrant and delicious.

When dawn arrived the following day, he saw that the water had been drawn up from beneath his grave. He felt a surge of nausea and vomited profusely, whereupon he realized that all phenomena are but the mind (*sarvadharma-mātracittatā*).
He then returned to his own country to compose his treatises. All of this was directly perceived through immediate cognition (*pratyakṣa*).
This is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for inference (*anumāna*), it is to observe a meaning by means of various signs and to know it through analogy.
Among all metaphors, the metaphor of a dream is the most pertinent. Just as what is seen in a dream—mountains, rivers, people, and things—is myriad and diverse in a thousand ways.
None of these are apart from the dreaming mind that conceives of a self; outside of this dreaming mind, not a single phenomenon can be found. This very point can be understood through analogy:
all phenomena presently manifesting are merely the manifestation of mind alone. As for the authoritative word of the Sages, it is said:
"The three realms are mind-only; all phenomena are consciousness-only. Thus do thousands of sutras and tens of thousands of treatises proclaim.
The determination that "mind-only" is the ultimate conclusion is finished. II.
Distinguishing and Clarifying "Complete Creation" through the Two Gates of Principle and Phenomena.

Regarding the phrase "distinguishing and clarifying complete creation": "complete" (jù) refers to complete possession according to principle; "creation" (zào) refers to actual creation according to phenomena. It is precisely this single thought-moment of mind.
Within [the mind], the ten realms and myriad phenomena are inherently present. This very single thought-mind, following conditions, is able to create the ten realms and myriad phenomena.
"Inherent presence" (*li-jù*) is like the principle that gold inherently possesses the potential to be fashioned into vases, plates, hairpins, or bracelets; "actual creation" (*shi-zào*) is...
It is like the conditions of a craftsman, a furnace, and a hammer, which produce vessels such as jars, plates, hairpins, and bracelets.

Furthermore, there is "inherent principle" (*li-jù*), which is like the inherent potential within flour to become various kinds of food; and there is "actualized production" (*shi-zào*), which is like the conditions of water, fire, and human labor that actually produce those various foods.
Because of the inherent principle, actualized production occurs; if the principle did not exist...

[The nature of] being endowed. What is it that constitutes phenomena? It is because they are endowed by principle that there is the creation of phenomena. Apart from the endowment of principle, there is no separate creation of phenomena.
It is through the existence of the creation of phenomena that the endowment of principle is revealed. If phenomena were not created, how could one know of the endowment of principle?

Therefore, the creation of phenomena is nothing other than the creation of the endowment of principle; apart from the creation of phenomena, there is no separate endowment of principle. Thus has the "endowment" been explained.
The composition is finished.
III. Distinguishing and Determining the True and the False by Examining the Identity and Difference of Names and Entities.

Regarding the distinction and determination of the true and the false: within the Buddha-dharma, there are cases where names are identical but entities differ, and there are cases where names differ but entities are the same.
Regarding "the same": this refers to the identity of name while the substance differs. For example, the single term "mind" (citta) has various aspects:

there is the physical heart-mass (*māṃsa-guḍa-citta*), the mind that perceives and contemplates (*ālambana-manasikāra-citta*), the mind that accumulates and arises (*cita-udaya-citta*), and the mind that is solid and substantial (*dṛḍha-sāra-citta*). The physical heart-mass is identical to the external four great elements; it possesses no capacity for cognition.

The "mind that cogitates" (*ālambana-citta*) pertains to all eight consciousnesses, because all eight types of consciousness are capable of cognizing their respective objects; this is thus a combination of the delusory and the real.

The "mind that accumulates and gives rise" (*saṃcita-utpāda-citta*) refers exclusively to the eighth [consciousness], because it can accumulate the seeds of all phenomena and give rise to the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of all phenomena;
this is thus a union of the real and the delusory. The "firm and solid mind" (*dṛḍha-hṛdaya*) is precisely the firm...
The nature of reality is non-conceptual, luminous awareness, the essence of the pure mind. What is here termed "mind-only" refers specifically to this firm, solid, and pure mind.

As for the phrase "different names but the same substance," it refers to the various ultimate designations taught in the various sūtras—such as *tathatā* (true thusness), *buddhadhātu* (buddha-nature), *bhūtalakṣaṇa* (real aspect), and *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm)—all of which are this very [firm mind].
This is indeed the true, pure mind. The distinction between the real and the false is hereby concluded.
IV. Regarding the "compromise and pointing out" based on the primordially existing and presently manifest [mind]:
as for this "compromise and pointing out," it is because all sutras state that the true mind has existed primordially from the beginningless past. Now, since...
It is said that it has existed from the beginning. How could it not exist right now? That which exists manifestly at present is precisely what has existed from the beginning.

If there were no beginninglessness, there would be no manifestation before us; and if one were apart from what is manifest before us, how could there be beginninglessness? Therefore, there is no need to exalt "existence from the beginning" or to trace back to a remote beginninglessness.
Rather, the self-nature of this very thought-moment of the present is the true mind that has existed from the beginning.

Thus, this present single thought-moment is entirely true yet constitutes delusion; entirely deluded yet is precisely the truth. Throughout the day one follows conditions, yet throughout the day there is no change.
Apart from this present single thought-moment, how could there be any other true mind to be found?
An ancient worthy said: "That which lies beyond the limit of Vītarāga is not separate from the gateway of the present world.

The active ignorance of sentient beings is precisely the substance of the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas. This comes close to the truth. Through the four preceding meanings, the principle of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*) is revealed;
therefore, the first [section] takes Mind-Only as its primary tenet. The direct demonstration of Mind-Only is hereby concluded.

II. Progressively Clarifying that All Dharmas Are [Mind] Regarding the progressive clarification that all dharmas are [mind]: furthermore, even a single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha" takes the Buddha alone as its primary principle.
Since all myriad dharmas are manifestations of the mind, they are in their entirety nothing but mind. Mind has no duality of self and other; mind has no boundaries or divisions.

Regarding the ten realms and the myriad phenomena—whether bases or objects, provisional names or substantial dharmas—whichever single phenomenon one may take up, it is the entire substance of the mind and possesses the great function of the mind.
Just as the mind is horizontally pervasive, so too does it vertically exhaust [all existence].
This is established by the principle of "mind-only": it is only form, only sound, only fragrance, only taste, only touch, and only mental objects, even unto only...
"Micro-dusts; only mustard seeds. When all things are established through their meanings alone, then for the first time the principle of 'Mind-Only' is truly realized.
If all things were not established through their meanings alone, there would be only the empty name of 'Mind-Only' without the actual reality of Mind-Only.
Because all things are established through their meanings alone, it is said that phenomena have no fixed characteristics. Upon encountering..."
The "condition" (pratyaya) is the thesis (pakṣa). Even [theories] such as "only atoms" or "only mustard seeds" may still serve as a thesis;
yet the Amitābha of the fruition-ground, adorned with the eighty thousand marks and signs, conversely cannot be taken as the thesis. Therefore, "only Buddha" is established as the thesis.
This concludes the second section, which further clarifies the myriad dharmas.
Third, absolute interpenetration and perfect fusion.
As for "absolute interpenetration and perfect fusion," even a single phrase such as "Amitābha Buddha" takes this absolute interpenetration and perfect fusion as its central principle.
Within the myriad phenomena of the ten realms, whichever phenomenon one may select, it is none other than the entire substance of the mind, endowed with the great function of the mind.
Transversely it pervades the ten directions; vertically it exhausts the three periods of time. It is free from the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations.

Its solitary essence is entirely true, with nothing existing outside of it. Pervasive and pure, there is no room for anything else within. Since this is the case for a single dharma, so it is for all dharmas.
Each, in relation to its own nature, is inherently free from dependence and has no exterior; this is what is meant by "transcending dependence. Furthermore, by means of the ten...
The myriad phenomena of the realms each pervade one another and each contain one another; they interlace one by one and penetrate one another through and through.
They are mutually unobstructed and unhindered, each remaining distinct without being corrupted or confused.

It is like the reflections appearing in layers within an ancient mirror on a high terrace, or like the thousand pearls of Indra’s net, revolving and mutually encompassing one another. This is described in terms of all phenomena looking toward one another.
This is what is meant by "perfect interfusion" (*yuanrong*). Now, we combine "absolute transcendence" (*juedai*) and "perfect interfusion" into a single school.

At the very moment of absolute transcendence, there is perfect interfusion; at the very moment of perfect interfusion, there is absolute transcendence. It is not that perfect interfusion exists separately apart from absolute transcendence—absolute transcendence is its very perfection and interfusion.
Nor is it that absolute transcendence exists separately apart from perfect interfusion—perfect interfusion is its very absolute transcendence.
Each is independently perfect and harmonious, and each is inconceivable. Now, to unify them all into a single school is the most inconceivable of the inconceivable.
Third, the section on independent perfection and harmony concludes.
