"Transcending emotion and departing from views" means that, by regarding all phenomena as beyond dependence, free from error, and devoid of negation, one has already transcended the emotional, deluded attachments of all sentient beings, as well as the various distinctions in the perceptions of the worthy and sages of the Three Vehicles. If one regards all phenomena...

Perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*). It completely encompasses the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and harmonizes the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). It is especially beyond the reach of ordinary sentiments or sagely views;

therefore, it establishes "transcending sentiment and departing from view" as its central tenet (*zong*). First, it takes "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) as its tenet. Second, it takes "Buddha-only" as its tenet.
Third, it takes "unconditioned perfect interfusion" as its tenet. Finally, it takes "transcending sentiment and departing from view" as its tenet.
Taken together, these four layers of fundamental principles constitute the true essence of the single phrase of the Amitābha school; how could they be easily explained?
This concludes the third section, which clarifies the fundamental principles.
○ Fourth, Manifesting the Superior Benefits:
One first attains the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and subsequently the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); following this, one realizes the Path of Fruition (*niṣṭhā-mārga*).

This is the common path of a thousand sages and an immutable, settled doctrine established throughout the ages. Yet, how easy is it to speak of the Path of Seeing? If one follows the teachings of the Vehicle (*yāna*)...

One must certainly achieve a great opening of circular understanding; if following the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), one must directly penetrate the heavy barrier before one may discuss the cultivation of the Way.
Otherwise, it becomes blind cultivation and reckless training, inevitably resulting in bumping into walls, striking against barriers, falling into pits, and tumbling into ditches.
Only the single gate of the Pure Land is not thus: from here to the west, passing through ten trillion Buddha-lands...
There is a world named Sukhāvatī. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.
Merely by making a vow and holding his name, one will immediately attain rebirth there. This is a realm personally known and personally seen by the Buddha’s own heart and eyes;
it is not something that can be known or seen by the worthy ones and sages of the Three Vehicles. One should simply [cultivate this] deeply...

Believing the Buddha’s words, one should make vows and recite the Name based upon them; this is to take the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as one’s own knowledge and vision, and there is no need to seek a separate gateway to enlightenment.
Furthermore, in other gateways for cultivating the Way, one must first attain awakening and then practice according to the Dharma.
By gathering the mind, one achieves meditative concentration (*samādhi*); based on concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) arises; and based on wisdom, afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed.
The wisdom that arises may be superior or inferior, and the afflictions that are severed may be shallow or deep; only then can one discuss whether there is regression or non-regression.
Only within this gateway of the Pure Land, by means of the mind of faith and aspiration alone, one single-mindedly upholds the Name.
When the practice reaches the state of "one-pointedness without distraction," the pure karma is fully perfected. After death, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. Once rebirth is attained—
One will then never again fall back. Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the path through other gates, one must first repent for one's present karma.

If present karma is not repented, it will constitute an obstruction to the Way, and there will be no path for further progress. Those who cultivate the practice of purity attain rebirth while still carrying their karma and do not need to repent for it;
by reciting the Buddha’s name with a sincere mind even once, one can extinguish eighty billion [kalpas of] karmic offenses.
This is because of the heavy offenses of birth and death throughout kalpas. Furthermore, when practicing the Way through other gates, one must sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

If even a fraction of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā*) remains unexhausted, then the birth and death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) will not be ended, and one cannot escape the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
Only those who practice the Pure Land method transcend the Triple World horizontally without severing the afflictions, departing from this Land of Common Dwelling.
One is born there to dwell together with them. Once born in that land, the very roots of birth and death are forever severed.
Having been born in that land, one constantly beholds the Buddha and hears the Dharma from time to time; clothing, food, and dwelling arise spontaneously.
The water birds and the forest trees all preach the Dharma. Dwelling together within this land, one horizontally perceives the three higher lands.
All the superior virtuous ones assemble in one place and perfectly realize the three kinds of non-retrogression; in a single lifetime, they immediately attain the rank of a Buddha.
Thus, the single gate of the Pure Land is the initial shortcut for seeking the gate of awakening; at the end, it does not require waiting for the development of wisdom, nor does it require [effort].
This repentance of karma does not require the severing of afflictions; it is the ultimate in brevity and essentiality, and the ultimate in directness and swiftness.

When its realization is attained, it is the ultimate in vastness and the ultimate in finality. Students should contemplate and savor this with a meticulous mind, making careful and detailed selections.
Do not, out of temporary pride, lose sight of this most excellent and supreme benefit. The explanation of the manifest superior benefits is concluded. Great.
The detailed exposition of the Pure Land is hereby concluded.

Part Two: Explaining Birth and Non-birth, which is further divided into three sections: first, according to the teachings; second, distinguishing and subsuming; third, refuting and establishing. Now, the first section.

Regarding the explanation in terms of the four teachings (*catvāra upadeśāḥ*): all four teachings possess the meaning of both arising and non-arising. If one does not carefully discern this, there is the fault of treating them as a single, undifferentiated whole.

Regarding the explanation in terms of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching, the fundamental principle states: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.

One attains the truth through the cessation [of these phenomena], yet this cessation is not itself the ultimate truth. If even cessation is not the truth, [how much less so are the phenomena themselves].
How much more so for the truths of suffering, its origin, and the path; the ultimate truth lies beyond the causal phenomena of these matters.

Therefore, according to the Mahāyāna teachings, it is judged to be the "partial truth" of non-arising. Regarding the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika-yāna), it is said: "All dharmas do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another."
It is not shared [with others], nor is it without cause; therefore, it is said to be "unborn" (*anutpāda*). Understanding that suffering is without suffering, one finds the True Reality (*satya*).
If even suffering is itself the Truth, how much more so its origin, cessation, and the path? This is precisely the unbornness of the True Reality.

According to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*), True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) do not change as they follow conditions; they are undefiled while within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), yet neither are they pure when realizing *nirvāṇa*.
It utterly transcends the two extremes and is not identical with any phenomena; this is the "Middle Only" (but-mid) of non-arising.

According to the Perfect Teaching, the Tathāgata-garbha is unchanging yet follows conditions, and following conditions yet remains unchanging. Whatever single phenomenon one grasps, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. It does not decrease in the ordinary person, nor does it increase in the sage. This is...

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one perfectly transcends the four propositions and perfectly encompasses the four propositions; this is the inconceivable non-arising (*anutpāda*). This concludes the section on the analysis according to the teachings.
II. Distinguishing and Subsuming.
Regarding the phrase "discerning and including": this means discerning and setting aside the three preceding [teachings] on non-arising, and including them within the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng).

Why is this? In the Tripitaka Teaching, it is said that once birth-and-death has ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. Here, "birth-and-death" refers to the phenomena of birth-and-death within the twenty-five realms of existence;
"quiescent extinction" refers to the arising of the partial truth of *nirvāṇa*. "Non-arising" lies beyond birth-and-death.
Regarding this treatise’s discussion of birth as non-birth: it is precisely the non-birth within birth; therefore, it does not accord with the intent of the Tripitaka Teaching.
Although the Shared Teaching speaks of birth as being non-birth, those who fail to grasp its true meaning ultimately fall into the fruit of annihilationism.
Furthermore, while the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings do not speak of Buddha-lands in other directions, this treatise concerns birth in the pure lands of other directions.
This is precisely non-arising; therefore, it is not the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

Although the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) speaks of Buddha-lands in other directions, its Middle Way principle does not coincide with the two extremes. This treatise’s discussion of arising and non-arising refers to arising that is the two extremes being identical to the Middle Way’s non-arising;
therefore, it is also not the meaning of the Distinct Teaching. Only the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) [is so].

The principle within this is precisely the dharma of birth in the four lands. Its very substance is the Middle Way; it is perfectly free from the four propositions and perfectly fuses the four propositions.
This means that birth is itself non-birth; it is both birth and non-birth; it is neither birth nor non-birth.
To raise one is to include all four, and the entirety of the four is one. Therefore, it is called "inconceivable."
The non-arising of this [rebirth] is precisely the fundamental tenet of this treatise; hence it is titled *The Treatise on Rebirth in the Pure Land as Non-arising*. III.
Refutation and Establishment:

Regarding refutation and establishment, there are those among worldly people who are biasedly attached to the existence of birth, those biasedly attached to non-arising, and those biasedly attached to existence...
Birth still possesses the benefit of rebirth in the Pure Land; yet those who cling exclusively to the doctrine of non-birth fundamentally fall into the delusions of conditioned shadows.
Taking this as "Mind-Only Pure Land" and "Self-Nature Amitābha," I have therefore titled this work *The Treatise on Birth in the Pure Land and Non-Birth*.
It is intended precisely to refute the false illusions of conditioned shadows and to establish birth in the Pure Land as being identical to the nature of the mind.
...of non-arising. Thus, an ancient worthy said: "If it arises, it definitely arises; if it departs, it truly does not depart. He further said:
"The dharmas produced by causes and conditions—I say they are emptiness, yet they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
The following passage in the treatise says: "The mind is complete and creates; how could there be a distinction between subject and object? The mind itself is the Buddha. It is...

The Buddha is the mind; the mind itself is the land, and the land itself is the mind. Both the causal conditions that create and the phenomena created are, in their very place, entirely the nature of the mind.
Therefore, to clarify this school and seek birth in the Land of Bliss is the supreme path wherein birth and non-birth are both merged in obscurity.
The explanation of birth and non-birth is complete.
Third, the explanation of the term for "treatise" (*upadeśa*):
in Sanskrit, it is *upadeśa*, which here is translated as "discourse on meaning" (*lunyi*). The *Liewang shu* states: "It refers to questioning, debating, investigating, and analyzing;
it means to dissect, judge, reveal, and instruct so that one may attain certainty. Questioning, debating, investigating, and analyzing constitute the "pedagogical treatise" (*jiaolun*). Dissecting...

To sever [delusions] and provide exposition is the practice of the treatise (*śāstra*). To bring about certainty is the principle of the treatise. Furthermore, questioning, debating, investigating, and analyzing constitute the teaching, practice, and principle of the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) within the stage of names.

To dissect, sever, and provide exposition constitutes the teaching, practice, and principle of the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the stage of semblance to contemplative practice.
To bring about certainty constitutes the teaching, practice, and principle of the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within the stage of partial realization.
Regarding principle: it is a discourse on the world-truth (loka-siddhānta). Regarding practice: it is a discourse on the truth for individuals and as an antidote (pudgala-pratipakṣa-siddhānta).
Regarding principle: it is a discourse on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-siddhānta). The explanation of the title of the treatise is concluded.
The second [section] explains that "Master Ming" (明) is the name of a kingdom; when the Zhu family possessed the empire, it was called the Great Ming (大明).
Mount Tiantai is a mountain in Zhejiang Province, located to the north of Taizhou Prefecture. Youxi is a place name situated within the mountain range. Śramaṇa...

This term is a transliteration from the Sanskrit; it is also called *sāman*. These are merely different Sanskrit pronunciations. Master Kumārajīva stated that whether one follows the Buddha-dharma or is a non-Buddhist, anyone who has left the household life is called a *śramaṇa*.
This is thus the general designation for those who have renounced the world. It may also be translated as "one who quiets the mind."
The *Śūramgama-sūtra* (Ruìyìng jīng) states: "One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa. It also says:

"Diligent Quieting," meaning to diligently seek precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, while extinguishing greed, anger, and delusion. Now, regarding the śramaṇas, there are four types of teachings, each divided into four categories:

the śramaṇa who excels in the Path (*mārgajina*), the śramaṇa who expounds the Path (*mārgadeśaka*), the śramaṇa who lives by the Path (*mārgajīvika*), and the śramaṇa who defiles the Path (*mārgadūṣika*).

If one diligently seeks the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings (*zàngtōng*), stills the mind of views and afflictions (*jìnsī*), and realizes the fruits of the Three Vehicles, such a person is a śramaṇa of the superior path of the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings.

If one arises from the ultimate truth (*zhēn*) to manifest in response (*yìng*), preaching the two types of Four Noble Truths—those of arising-and-ceasing (*shēngmiè*) and non-arising (*wúshēng*)—such a person is a śramaṇa of the path of teaching (*shuōdào*).
If one receives these two teachings and cultivates the seven categories of the factors of enlightenment (*dàopǐn*), such a person is a śramaṇa of the living path (*huódào*).

"Śramaṇa," it is said; otherwise, one is a śramaṇa who defiles the Way. This applies equally to the Separate and Perfect Teachings. "Chuan-deng" (Lamp of Transmission) is the name of the Master of the Treatise;
it means the transmission of the lamp of the True Truth, the lamp of the Conventional Truth, the lamp of the Middle Truth, the lamp of the Gradual Teaching, and the lamp of the One Mind.
Now, in composing this treatise, I transmit the Western [Land of] Mind-Only, the four lands, the self-nature, and the three bodies. One...
The mind is the wondrous lotus lamp. *Vandana* (和南) is, in Sanskrit, *vandana-mai* or *vandana*; it is erroneously transliterated as *he-nan*.
It is translated as "I prostrate," which refers to bowing in worship. *Zhuàn* (撰) means to compose or to create.
The Great Master’s secular surname was Ye; he was a native of Quzhou in Zhejiang. In his youth, he left home [to become a monk] under the Chan Master Ying’an of Jinxian. Following...

He visited Master Baisong and heard him lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Suddenly, he experienced a profound spiritual resonance. He then inquired about the essential meaning of the "Great Samādhi" of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

Master Baisong stared at him with wide eyes and looked him over intently; at that moment, Tan Deng entered into realization. Baisong bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* robe from the Jin-yun collection.
For the rest of his life, he practiced the repentance rites of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahākaruṇā*, the *Prabhāsa*, the *Amitābha*, and the *Śūraṅgama*. There was no [other practice].
On the day of the *xū* (void) stem, he chose to reside at Gaoming Temple by the secluded stream. Previously, a local man named Ye Qi had buried his parents behind the temple.
He dreamed of a deity who said, "This is a site for the Path of the Sages. A flesh-and-blood Bodhisattva is about to perform great Buddhist works here;

you must move [the remains] quickly. Qi did not believe him. Soon thereafter, his entire family fell ill and was in distress. Frightened, he moved them. The following day, Denglü arrived. It was then that—

This site established the ancestral temple of the Tiantai school, where disciples gathered like the spokes of a wheel. Once, before the Great Buddha of Xinchang, he ascended the seat to expound the principles;
the assembly heard the resonant sounds of celestial music from within the stone chamber.

When his lecture concluded, he passed away into stillness, yet he composed this treatise to harmonize the three contemplations (*sanzhuan*) and propagate the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. Every year, he practiced the four samādhis, setting a personal example for others.
He led the assembly with diligent and courageous resolve. He annotated such scriptures as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Whenever he took up the brush, he invariably wore his monastic robes. Over his career, he presided over more than seventy lecture series.

Foreknowing that the time had come, he wrote out the five characters of the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* with his own hand, then chanted the title of the scripture twice aloud before passing away in serene stillness. This concludes the general heading of the treatise.

II. Requesting the Bestowal of Blessings and Stating the Intent. This section has two parts: first, taking refuge and requesting blessings; second, the benefits of composing the treatise. Now, the first:
I prostrate to the Perfect Wisdom of the Muni, The Infinite Life Buddha, the Great Guide.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Mahāyāna Sūtra* as it was taught, The definitive meaning of the definitive, the most perfect and sudden;
The Wondrous Virtue of Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Great Ocean;
Asaṅga, Nāgārjuna, and Vasubandhu, And the patriarchs of the Lotus Society on Mount Lu in this land.

Tiantai Zhiyi and Fazhi— To the Dharma Masters who have propagated the teachings throughout past and present, I now take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem, Seeking their secret empowerment to awaken my spiritual consciousness and compose this treatise to propagate the Dharma.
Regarding the necessity of first taking refuge in the Triple Gem, there are briefly four meanings. First, to accord with the ancients.
First, it is because it is the ritual of the noble sages. Second, it is to cause the increase of the merit, fortune, and roots of goodness of sentient beings.

Third, it is because it differs from the discourses of non-Buddhists which lack a fundamental basis. Fourth, it reveals that both the one who takes refuge and the object of refuge are empty and quiescent by nature;

the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus is inconceivable. One must know that taking refuge involves both the one who takes refuge and the object of refuge; there is also the request for empowerment.

Regarding the one who requests and the one who is requested, first the capacity for taking refuge is clarified. In the text, "prostrating" (*kai-shou*) refers to bowing with the head touching the ground;

this is an action of the body (*kāya-karman*) that encompasses all three modes of action (*trividha-karman*). Furthermore, "taking refuge in life" (*gui-ming*) means that both body and life are surrendered as a place of reliance.

"Taking refuge" (*gui*) carries the meanings of casting oneself toward [the object] and returning [to it]. Within the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), only the merit of the Triple Gem (*triratna*) can serve as a support.
Therefore, one should take refuge in the essential nature of the Triple Gem, which is precisely the subtle, momentary mind-nature present before all sentient beings.
Since beginningless time, they have turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the sensory dust, willingly fleeing from and turning away from it;

now, by turning away from the dust and conforming to awakening, they restore the source of the original mind—hence it is called "returning. As for "life," this is a provisional designation established based upon the uninterrupted continuity of form and mind.
There is no such thing as a truly existent dharma; it is merely that which sentient beings, in their deluded minds, hold most precious.

Following worldly convention, this term is used to encompass the three types of action (*trikarma*). When one casts this most precious life toward the Three Jewels of the Sustaining Community (*saṃgha*), it serves as a superior condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
By investigating this provisionally established life, its fundamental basis is found to be ungraspable; thus, one returns [to the source].

This is the Three Jewels as a single essence. Regarding "The Benevolent One" (*Nengren*) and below, these are the Three Jewels to which one takes refuge. Furthermore, there are three parts: first, the elucidation of the Buddha Jewel;

second, the elucidation of the Dharma Jewel; and third, the elucidation of the Sangha Jewel. "The Benevolent One of Perfect Wisdom" and "The Great Teacher of Immeasurable Life and Enlightenment" refer to the Buddha Jewel.
The first phrase clarifies the Teacher of this land, while the second phrase refers to the Teacher of that land. [In Sanskrit...]
Śākyamuni. This is translated as "The Benevolent Sage of Silent Stillness. "Benevolent" (Nengren) represents great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), signifying that he does not abide in *nirvāṇa*.

"Silent Stillness" (Jimo) represents great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), signifying that he does not abide in *saṃsāra*. Thus, this auspicious title was established to denote the simultaneous operation of both compassion and wisdom.
Furthermore, "Benevolent" (Nengren) is his clan name. As stated in the Āgamas: Long ago there was a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) of the Ikṣvāku clan, who favored his secondary consort...

Because of these slanders, the four princes were banished to the north of the Snowy Mountains. There they established cities and settled; through their virtue, people flocked to them. Within a few years, they had become a powerful nation.
The father king, filled with regret and remembrance, dispatched an envoy to summon them. The four sons declined on account of their transgressions and did not return.
The father king sighed three times, saying, "My son is Śākya," and thus the clan was named after him. It is also said that he dwelt beneath a straight tree (*ṛju-vṛkṣa*).
He was named Śākya because he was born in a grove; since the kingdom was established in that grove, the family took "Grove" (Śāka) as its surname, while "Silent One" (Muni) was his personal name.
The *Buddhacarita-sūtra* states: Furthermore, the members of the Śākya clan were by nature arrogant and talkative, yet upon seeing the Prince...

Everyone remained silent. The King said, "He should be named Muni. Furthermore, "Able One" (Muni) signifies great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which consists of compassion for sentient beings (*sattvālambana-karuṇā*), compassion for phenomena (*dharmālambana-karuṇā*), and objectless compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*).
"Silent and Still" signifies great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), which consists of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Now, the three types of compassion are perfected and the three types of wisdom are fulfilled. These three compassions constitute merit (*puṇya*).
The adornment of virtue; the three types of wisdom constitute the adornment of wisdom. When merit and wisdom are both perfected, they adorn the Dharma-body; thus he is called Śākyamuni.
As for "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus), he is the guide who receives and leads beings in that land. The *Yāojie* states:
"In the Sanskrit language, Amitābha is correctly translated as 'Immeasurable. Its essence is ineffable. The Original Teacher [Śākyamuni], by means of his light and life..."
There are two meanings that encompass all immeasurables: "Life" (*āyuṣ*) is vertical, exhausting the three periods of time; "Light" (*prabhā*) is horizontal, pervading the ten directions.

When the horizontal and vertical mutually penetrate, this is the very substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Now, when we speak of "Immeasurable Life," we cite the vertical to include the horizontal.

As for "Awakening" (*bodhi*), it refers to self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of awakening—realizing that the nature is truly eternal and understanding that delusions are empty and false.
To awaken for oneself is called "self-awakening. To exercise non-referential compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) and deliver the realm of sentient beings is called "awakening others.

To exhaust the source and reach the ultimate depth, such that practice is perfected and fruition is fulfilled, is called "fulfillment of awakening. As for the "Great Teacher," the Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*) to guide beings;

when a practitioner reaches the stage of "semblance" within contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), they are no longer disturbed by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and thus they perceive Amitābha.

The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and its assembly of noble ones lead [beings] back to the two types of pure lands: the Land of Common Residence (*sāmbhogikakṣetra*) and the Land of Expedient Means (*upāyakṣetra*).
When one reaches the stage of partial realization, being undisturbed by the two extremes, one thus experiences the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and its assembly of noble ones.
They are led back to the two kinds of pure lands: the Land of True Reward and the Land of Tranquil Light.

Furthermore, because the Buddha possesses forty-eight kinds of great vows and is universally guided by means of the three bodies, he is called the Great Guide. This concludes the section on the Buddha Jewel. Second, the Dharma Jewel is explained.

Regarding "that which is taught": the Buddha is the teacher, and the sūtra is that which is taught. Regarding "Peaceful Nurturing" (An-yang): in Sanskrit it is called *Sukhāvatī*, which here means "Peaceful Nurturing";
it is also called "Pure Tranquility" (*Qingtai*) or "Ultimate Bliss" (*Jile*). This refers to being eternally free from all suffering and attaining the foremost state of security.
Regarding "Mahāyāna": "Great" (*Dà*) is spoken in contrast to "Small. It possesses the three greatnesses of essence (*svabhāva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*).
The Lotus Sūtra states: "The chariot is high and wide, adorned with various jewels. Because the chariot is high, it is said to be great in essence (*tǐ*);

because the chariot is wide, it is said to be great in characteristics (*xiàng*); because it is adorned with various jewels, it is said to be great in function (*yòng*). "Vehicle" (*chéng*) refers to a carriage.

It is named according to its metaphor and defined by its function of conveying [beings]. There are three types: the Vehicle of Principle (*li-cheng*), the Vehicle of Accordance (*sui-cheng*), and the Vehicle of Attainment (*de-cheng*).

The greatness of essence (*ti-da*) constitutes the Vehicle of Principle; the greatness of characteristics (*xiang-da*) constitutes the Vehicle of Accordance; and the greatness of function (*yong-da*) constitutes the Vehicle of Attainment. Furthermore, the three greatnesses that are the object of conveyance constitute the Vehicle of Principle;
the three wisdoms that are the agent of conveyance constitute the Vehicle of Accordance; and the ultimate perfection of both agent and object constitutes the Vehicle of Attainment. (From the *Sūtra*)
"Sūtra" in Sanskrit is translated here as "Kie-king" (Sūtra). This means "conforming to conditions," "conforming to events," and "conforming to principles.
Conforming to conditions refers to the Sūtras of Teaching; conforming to events refers to the Sūtras of Practice; and conforming to principles refers to the Sūtras of Principle.

Furthermore, because they conform to conditions, they are Sūtras of the Worldly Universal Truth (loka-saṃvṛti-satya); because they conform to events, they are Sūtras of the Two Universal Truths: the Personal (pudgala) and the Remedial (pratipakṣa).

It accords with principle; therefore, it is a sūtra of the ultimate *siddhānta*. "Definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*) refers to the clear and thorough understanding of the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and the principle of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
As for this principle being clearly understood, the realization of the Buddha-dharma realm exhaustively penetrates this principle.

To clarify the meaning of "definitive" (*nītārtha*): the various sutras on the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) are fully endowed with both the principle (*li*) and the phenomenon (*shi*) of the definitive;

therefore, they are called "the definitive among the definitive. Regarding the "perfect and sudden" (*yuan-dun*): this refers to the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). It is called "perfect" because it possesses four meanings:
perfect subtlety, perfect fusion, perfect sufficiency, and perfect suddenness. Now, within every thought-moment of the Pure Land Dharma-gate, there is perfect transformation.

Thus we know that from their initial resolve, there are none among themselves or others who do not practice; and from their subsequent resolve, there are none among themselves or others who do not enter [enlightenment].

This refers to the passage below concerning the single thought-moment of the nature of mind, which perfectly encompasses the principle of the three truths, and is realized through the perfect threefold contemplation.
"Entering" refers to what is called the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*). "To elucidate" means to bring forth and clarify.
Regarding "birth in the Pure Land as non-birth," this means that all phenomena produced by causes and conditions are, in their entirety, the Middle Way of non-birth.

[The text] universally intends for future generations to awaken to this gate, severing doubt and giving rise to faith so as to reach the stage of non-retrogression. Although doubts are immeasurable, they are generally categorized into three types.
First is perverse doubt: believing only in the illusory nature of conditioned reflections, yet failing to believe that the Buddha-lands are mind-only.
Second is partial doubt: believing only in the truth of biased emptiness, yet remaining ignorant of the conventional reality of wondrous existence. Third is gradual doubt.

One merely believed in and cultivated the gradual unfolding of virtuous qualities, yet did not know the horizontal pervasiveness of the inherent nature of virtue. Now, by awakening to this gate, one severs perverse doubt and gives rise to right faith;
one severs partial doubt and gives rise to perfect faith; one severs gradual doubt and gives rise to sudden faith. There are three kinds of non-retrogression:

first, non-retrogression in status, wherein one enters the stream of the sages and does not fall back into the realm of ordinary beings; second, non-retrogression in practice, wherein one constantly delivers sentient beings.
They do not fall into the stages of the two vehicles; their three mindfulnesses never regress, and mind-moment after mind-moment they flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Now, entering this gate, in every thought-moment they perfectly sever the three doubts, perfectly give rise to the three faiths, and perfectly realize the three non-regressions.
The second section, the request for an exposition of the intent, is concluded.
○ Third, the classification of topics and establishment of the treatise. This contains two parts: first, the classification of topics; second, the establishment of the treatise. ○ Now, the first.

In composing this treatise, ten gates are established: first, the gate of the true dharma-realm; second, the gate of the dependent origination of body and land; third, the gate of the mutual identity of mind and land;
fourth, the gate of the non-duality of sentient beings and Buddhas; fifth, the gate of the dharma-realm as mindfulness; sixth, the gate of the mutual swallowing of object and contemplation;
seventh, the gate of the naturalness of the three contemplations; eighth, the gate of spontaneous resonance; ninth, the gate of the eternal... [the text continues].
The first gate: the gate of the mutual presence of the ten [realms] in the present and future.

Cheshu said: "The general purport of the ten gates is as follows: the first clarifies the inherent nature (*li-jù*); the second clarifies phenomenal creation (*shi-zào*). The former two are the general [principles]."

The latter eight constitute the specific [teachings]. Among the first three and the fourth gates, the former two primarily manifest the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*), while the fifth and subsequent gates primarily manifest the cultivation-endowment (*bhāvanā-guṇa*).
The ninth gate discusses them horizontally, while the tenth discusses them vertically. Nevertheless, among these, the fifth gate alone is the most essential;
for regarding the meanings of phenomena and principle, the general and the specific, nature and cultivation, horizontal and vertical, and so forth, none are excluded from this single thought-moment.
Because it is the entirety of the Dharma-realm, if a student can thoroughly clarify this single gate, then all preceding and subsequent gates are fully contained within it.
Furthermore, the reason these ten categories are all termed "gates" (mōn) is that a gate has the meaning of "being able to pass through";
that is to say, each of these ten gates allows for universal penetration. Below, the establishment of the treatise is clarified; first, the first [gate] is explained.
I. The First Gate: The Single True Dharma-realm. This further has two parts: first, the verse; second, the treatise. Now, for the first:

Within the single true dharma-nature, the ten dharma-realms are fully present. Because the primary and the derivative are fundamentally interfused, there is no distinction between the sentient beings who arise and the Buddhas.

This section clarifies the principle of inherent completeness (*li-jù*). It means that within the single thought-moment of a sentient being’s mind-nature, the three thousand aspects of reality (*sanqian shixiang*) are fundamentally complete.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: “Only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust the true nature of all phenomena (*zhufa shixiang*).

What is meant by the true nature of all phenomena? It refers to the fact that all phenomena possess such characteristics (*xiang*), such natures (*xing*), and so forth. This refers to within this very mind.
The ten dharma-realms are inherently present; each of these ten realms further possesses its own ten realms, collectively forming one hundred realms.
Within each realm, there are again the ten "thusnesses" (*yurushi*), thereby forming one thousand "thusnesses. Hence, it is said that there are "one hundred realms and one thousand thusnesses.

Furthermore, there are one thousand provisional names, one thousand real dharmas, and one thousand environments and retributions, which together constitute three thousand. These three thousand dharmas...
Apart from even a single moment of deluded mind—since the deluded mind is thus, so too are deluded objects.

Whatever one picks up, whether a fragrance, a flower, a speck of dust, or a sound, each is immediately the three thousandfold reality-phenomena (*trisāhasra-tathatā*). Therefore, the environment and its inhabitants are interfused; living beings and Buddhas are not distinct.

II. The Section on the Treatise is divided into two parts: first, the establishment of the thesis; second, the defense against objections. The first part [the establishment of the thesis] is further divided into three:
first, the general indication; second, the detailed explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first [the general indication]:
The Treatise says: The one true dharma-realm is precisely the fundamental mind-nature of sentient beings.
This mind-nature possesses immeasurable virtues and receives immeasurable names.

If one speaks in terms of the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*), then whichever single phenomenon (*dharma*) one picks up, it is immediately the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), possessing immeasurable virtues and receiving immeasurable names.

What is now called "the mind-nature of sentient beings" is an explanation from the perspective of contemplating the mind (*guanxin*); that is, there is no distinction between the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
If explained in terms of the Buddha-dharma, those of initial capacity would find it too lofty and thus harbor doubts; however, if explained in terms of sentient beings...

Regarding the phrase "arising phenomena": furthermore, fearing that [the scope] might be too broad, I shall explain it solely in terms of the sixth consciousness—the single thought-moment of the present.
This is both proximate and essential. As for "sentient beings," this refers to the provisional designation "sentient being" applied to the harmony of the five aggregates and the four great elements.

As for "originally existing," it means that they have not been non-existent from the beginning; it is merely given the name "existence" by force of convention. As for "the nature of the mind," it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; it is merely...

It is named "Mind" (citta); it illuminates while remaining eternally quiescent. It is provisionally named "Nature" (prakṛti). As for "virtue" (guṇa), it refers to the actual presence of functional capacity;
as for "name," it is a designation established in accordance with that capacity. This concludes the general overview.
II. Separate Explanation of the Two [Parts]. First, the inquiry and explanation regarding the possession of virtues; second, the inquiry and explanation regarding the receiving of the name.

The first [section] has four parts: first, the differentiation of the three virtues; second, the harmonization of the three virtues; third, the identification with the three truths; fourth, the citation of scriptures as proof. The first [of these four] has two parts:
first, the general indication; second, the specific elucidation. Now, the first [part]: the general indication.

How does one possess immeasurable virtues? To state the essentials: they are the substance of nature (*xingti*), the magnitude of nature (*xingliang*), and the inherent endowment of nature (*xingju*).

Second, the detailed explanation has three parts: first, explaining the substance of nature; second, explaining the magnitude of nature; third, explaining the inherent endowment of nature. Now, the first [part].
What is the essence of its nature? It refers to this mind-nature, which transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
Its essential nature is firm and solid, pure and untainted, neither arising nor ceasing, eternally abiding and indestructible.
"Transcending the four and severing the hundred" correctly reveals the essence (*tattva*). The four lines following "the nature of the essence" clarify its possession of attributes.

As for the four lines, they refer to the position of existence (*astitva*), the position of non-existence (*nāstitva*), the position of both existence and non-existence (*ubhayatva*), and the position of neither existence nor non-existence (*anubhayatva*).

The "hundred negations" refers to each of these four positions being further analyzed into four sub-positions; thus, four times four makes sixteen positions. When these are applied across the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*), they constitute forty-eight positions.
There are forty-eight phrases already arisen and forty-eight not yet arisen, which together constitute ninety-six phrases. Adding the four fundamental phrases makes one hundred phrases in total.

As for the term "detached and severed," it means that the essence of this nature is fundamentally detached from the characteristics of verbal expression, detached from the characteristics of names and words, and detached from the characteristics of mental objects. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "This Dharma is not something to be conceptualized."
It is that which can be understood through discernment. This means that once one falls into conceptualization and discrimination, one does not transcend the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).

If one clings to these four propositions, one falls into the heterodox views of the four propositions characteristic of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Prajñā is like a great mass of fire;
it cannot be touched from any of its four sides. To touch it is to be burned. Yet, it must also not be fixedly avoided, lest one fall into the extreme of nihilism.

Regarding the term "view" (*darśana*): if one can harmonize these [four], then Prajñā is like a cool, refreshing pond, through which all four gates are capable of entering the Way, thereby forming the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Furthermore, as for true emptiness:
from the very beginning, it is because it is not associated with any defiled dharmas, and because it is free from the differentiated characteristics of all dharmas."

Because there is no mind of false conceptualization, one should know that True Suchness (tathatā) is neither characterized by existence, nor by non-existence, nor by both existence and non-existence, nor by neither existence nor non-existence;

it is neither a single characteristic, nor diverse characteristics, nor both single and diverse characteristics, nor neither single nor diverse characteristics. To speak briefly: because all sentient beings falsely differentiate [it], [it appears otherwise].

A separate mind cannot contact it; therefore, it is established as emptiness (*śūnyatā*). According to the ultimate principle, deluded thoughts do not exist, and emptiness itself is empty, because that which is negated is non-existent and the negator is likewise non-existent.
Below, its possession of qualities is clarified: its essential nature is firm and stable, which is the quality of the Self (*ātman*).
"Self" has the meaning of sovereignty, for it is capable of being the master; thus, it cannot be destroyed, and for this reason it is so called.
Firm and concentrated. To manifest that the nature of mind is the sovereign of the ten realms and the myriad dharmas is the quality of purity (*śubha*);
this means the original nature is pure and free from the defilement of the five abodes of delusion. It is unborn and undying, the quality of bliss (*sukha*);

this means it is fundamentally devoid of the two kinds of birth-and-death—segmental and transformative—and is therefore eternally abiding and indestructible, the quality of permanence (*nitya*). Furthermore...
The four phrases each possess the four virtues; this concludes the clarification of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, the clarification of the scope of the nature (*dhātu*):

What is meant by the scope of the nature? It refers to this mind-nature, which vertically exhausts the three periods of time and horizontally pervades the ten directions. While worlds have boundaries, [the nature] has none.
Space is boundless; space has limits. The nature of the mind is boundless; the present has limits. The past and future are boundless;
the past and future have limits. The nature of the mind is boundless—exhaustively inexhaustible, immeasurably immeasurable.
Regarding the "three limits": the past, present, and future constitute the three periods of time (*tri-kāla*). The past also possesses three [divisions]:
namely, the past-of-the-past, the present-of-the-past, and the future-of-the-past. The present also possesses three:
namely, the past-of-the-present, the present-of-the-present, and the future-of-the-present. The future also possesses three: namely, the past-of-the-future... [and so forth].
The past, the future, and the present; the future of the future, plus one fundamental period, thus constitute ten periods. As the ancient masters said:

"Throughout the ten periods of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment. Therefore, it is said that vertically they exhaust the three time-intervals. Regarding the ten directions:
in terms of the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*), they are the ten realms; in terms of the environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-phala*), they are called the ten directions. Based on...

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is said that this ocean of worlds is supported by wind-circles as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru, which are able to sustain the fragrant water-ocean named Jewel Light Muni.
From this fragrant water-ocean emerges a great lotus flower called Various Radiant Filaments and Fragrance Banner; this world resides within it. This world is encircled by a diamond perimeter.
Within the mountains, throughout all the great earth, there are seas of fragrant water numbering as many as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Within each of these seas of fragrant water, there is a great lotus flower;
each lotus flower contains world-systems that abide therein. Within each world-system, there are twenty layers of Flower-Treasury worlds.

They are arranged in successive order. Although these ten times unspeakably many seas of fragrant water—equal in number to the atoms within Buddha-lands—are vast, they do not transcend the phenomenal aspect of the single thought-moment of the mind-nature; hence it is called the "boundless ocean of lands.

Since self and others are not separated by even the tip of a hair, it is said that [this ocean] "pervades the ten directions horizontally. This explains the four propositions regarding whether worlds have boundaries and so forth.

The meaning of horizontal pervasiveness: This refers to the fact that although there are many successive worlds within the seas of fragrant water, numbering as many as the atoms of all Buddha-fields above, none of them ever transcend the bounds of space; therefore, it is said that while worlds have limits, space is limitless.

As for "space has limits, but the nature of mind is limitless": this is because space possesses characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas the nature of mind is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). (From the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*)
The Sūtra says: "Emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. The myriad lands of out-flowing dust all depend upon emptiness for their birth.
When the bubble ceases, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three worlds? It further states: "The empty space of the ten directions..."
It arises within your mind like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky; therefore, it is said that while space has boundaries, the nature of the mind is boundless.
The four propositions beginning with "the present has boundaries" explain the meaning of "vertically exhausting [all time].
That "the present has boundaries" means that the past and future constitute the limits of the present. That "the past and future are boundless" means that the past and future...
Because it is inexhaustible, it transcends the limits of past and future. Regarding the boundlessness of the nature of mind, a sutra states:

"When the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. The arising of the mind constitutes the limit of the past, and the cessation of the mind constitutes the limit of the future.
Therefore, it is said that it transcends the limits of past and future. Since the nature of mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, it is called boundless.
"Inexhaustible and immeasurable" is the summary. The former phrase summarizes the vertical [dimension], and the latter phrase summarizes the horizontal [dimension].

"Inexhaustible" means not an inexhaustibility that is merely non-ending; rather, it is an inexhaustibility that transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations. "Immeasurable" is likewise so.
This concludes the elucidation of the nature and measure.
The third section clarifies the nature of inherent possession and has three parts: first, the clarification of provisional names; second, the clarification of primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*);
and third, the clarification of secondary retribution (*nirmāṇakāya*). Now, for the first part: regarding "provisional names," these refer to the individual names of the ten dharma-realms.
These names are established based upon the real dharmas of primary and secondary retribution. This includes the name of the Buddha, down to the name of the hell-dweller.
"Name" (字): In contrast to substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*), it is therefore called a "provisional name" (*prajñapti*).

What is meant by "inherent possession" (*xingju*)? It refers to this mind-nature, which possesses the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), namely: the Buddha-dharmadhātu and the Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu.
The dharma-realm of pratyekabuddhas, the dharma-realm of śrāvakas, the dharma-realm of devas, the dharma-realm of asuras, the dharma-realm of humans, the dharma-realm of animals,
the dharma-realm of hungry ghosts, and the dharma-realm of hell-beings— these are merely provisional designations.
This provisional designation is further explained in two parts: first, a brief explanation of the provisional designation; second, a brief elucidation of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

That which is said to be this "mind-nature" possessing the ten dharma-realms means that it possesses the provisional designations, the real dharmas, the dependent and retributive rewards, and the three thousand realms of existence.

In Sanskrit it is called *buddha*; here it is translated as "the Awakened One. This refers to awakening oneself, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakening. Awakening oneself distinguishes one from ordinary beings.

Awakening others distinguishes [the Buddha] from those of the Two Vehicles; awakening perfected distinguishes him from Bodhisattvas. The Buddha is thus one whose three types of awakening are complete and who is endowed with all myriad virtues;
therefore, he is called an "Awakened One" (*buddha*). In Sanskrit, he is called *bodhisattva*, which here means "one who awakens sentient beings.

From the perspective of his own practice (*svārtha*), although he has attained awakening, his emotional afflictions have not yet been entirely exhausted; hence, he is called an "awakening sentient being. From the perspective of transforming others (*parārtha*), he is for the sake of awakening [others].
This refers to the awakening of sentient beings. In Sanskrit, they are called *pratyekabuddha*, which translates here as "Solitary Realizer" (*yùanjué*). There are two types:
those who appear during the time of a Buddha and awaken to the Way by practicing the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination are called Solitary Realizers;

those who appear in a world without a Buddha and awaken spontaneously without a teacher are called Pratyekabuddhas (Self-Realizers). As for the term "Śrāvaka" (Voice-hearer), according to the Mahāyāna, it refers to those who—by means of the Buddha’s... [text continues]
Regarding "Śrāvaka" (道聲): because they cause all to hear [the Dharma], they are called Śrāvakas. In the Hīnayāna, one awakens to the Way by hearing the sounds of the Buddha’s Four Noble Truths;
hence, they are called Śrāvakas. *Devā* in Sanskrit means "Heaven" (天). "Heaven" refers to being naturally so (*t'ien-jan*);

because they constantly experience natural bliss, they are called Heaven. This includes the six heavens of the Desire Realm, the four dhyānas, and the four formless realms. *Brahmā* in Sanskrit... [text ends]
Asura. This is translated as "Not-Upright" (Wu-ndeng-zheng), meaning that while the males are ugly, the females are beautiful.

It is also translated as "Non-Gods" (Fei-tian), signifying those who resemble gods but are not gods. They comprise four categories: devas, humans, ghosts, and animals. In Sanskrit they are called *manuṣya*, which means "human.

A human (*manuṣya*) is so called because of "endurance" (*marṣa*); it refers to the ability to endure both adverse and favorable conditions. This term encompasses the four continents. In Sanskrit... [text continues].
*Tiryag-yoni* (底栗車): translated here as "animals" (*tiryak*). This includes the three types: those of water, land, and air. *Preta* (梵云閃多): translated here as "hungry ghosts" (*preta*).
This refers to those who possess wealth, those with little wealth, and those with no wealth at all. *Niraya* (梵云泥犂耶): translated here as "non-existence" (*niraya*).

This refers to the absence of pleasure and the presence of suffering. "Hell" (dīya) is a name established according to its meaning in this context; because it is a prison beneath the earth, it is called a "hell.

This category includes various distinctions such as the Great and Small Hells, and the Cold and Hot Hells. This is a brief explanation of the conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Second, regarding the explanation of the *dharmadhātu*, there are three meanings:
namely, that the ten numbers are the supported (*āśrita*), while the *dharmadhātu* is the support (*āśraya*). Thus, there is the relationship between the supported and the support.

They are collectively designated as such; therefore, they are called the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, within these ten dharma-realms, each has its own respective cause and its own respective fruit, without mutual confusion or intermixture;
therefore, they are called the ten dharma-realms. Moreover, each and every one of these ten dharmas is, in its very essence, a dharma-realm.
Therefore, we speak of the ten dharma realms. The explanation of provisional names is concluded.
II. Clarifying the primary retribution (vipāka).

Furthermore, there is primary retribution, namely: the five aggregates (*skandha*) of a Buddha, the five aggregates of a Bodhisattva, and so on, down to the five aggregates of those in hell. This is...
Regarding the actual dharma as the primary retribution (*vipāka*): this refers to the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) produced with ignorance as its cause and karma as its condition.

It is precisely this name-and-form that constitutes the primary retribution; therefore, it is called "primary retribution. As for the term "name-and-form," it refers to the eighth consciousness descending [into the womb].

At the time of conception, the consciousness-mind is without form and possesses only a name; therefore, it is called "name" (*nāma*). The father’s semen and the mother’s blood are phenomena with substance;
therefore, they are called "form" (*rūpa*). As for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), these two factors of name and form are expanded into five:

"name" is divided into the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; "form" is the aggregate of form itself. "Aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of "covering" or "obscuring," as it veils the Dharma-body.
Therefore, they are also called the five aggregates (*skandha*). "Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation; it refers to the accumulation of birth and death.

The Buddha’s five aggregates are the five aggregates of the dharma-nature, which are neither with-outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without-outflows (*anāsrava*); that is to say: true, wholesome, and wondrous form; the foremost right concentration;
unsurpassed wondrous wisdom; true liberation of nature; and all-encompassing knowledge and vision. As for the Bodhisattva’s five aggregates, they likewise consist of...
The five aggregates with outflows and without outflows; pure and impure forms; pleasant and unpleasant feelings; the formations of the notion of self and the notion of non-self;

the perceptions of permanence and impermanence; the outflow-free five aggregates of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—namely, morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
the wholesome, outflow-bound five aggregates of humans and devas; and the unwholesome, outflow-bound five aggregates of the four evil destinies. These...
These are the "real dharmas," which are spoken in contrast to provisional designations (*prajñapti*). This concludes the section on primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Third, the explanation of the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*):
Furthermore, there is dependent retribution, namely the lands of the Buddhas, the lands of the Bodhisattvas, and even the lands of the hells.

The "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*) refers to that upon which the sentient beings of the ten realms rely for their dwelling; furthermore, it is that which is evoked by the primary retribution (*mukhya-vipāka*).

As for the "Buddha-lands," this refers to the Pure Land of the Constant, Quiescent, and Radiant Light (*nitya-prasrabdha-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*) upon which the Buddha relies. The lands of the Bodhisattvas are divided into three types.
If it concerns Bodhisattvas of the Perfect or Distinct Teachings who have destroyed ignorance, they dwell in the Land of True Reward and also partially enter the Land of Quiescent Light.
If their afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) are exhausted, they rely on the Land of Expedient Means; if they are not yet exhausted, they dwell among humans and devas.
For Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching whose delusions are exhausted, they rely on the Land of Expedient Means; if they are not yet exhausted, they dwell among humans and devas.
Bodhisattvas dwell among humans and devas. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have exhausted their afflictions dwell by means of skillful means;
those who have not yet exhausted them dwell among humans and devas. Devas dwell in palaces; humans dwell upon the earth; asuras dwell at the bottom of the ocean or along its shores;
animals dwell upon the earth, in water, or in the air; pretas dwell in filth, excrement, or fire; [and those in] the eight cold hells...
The eight hot hells constitute the hell realms. Above these, each of the ten realms possesses ten aspects, totaling one hundred realms.

Furthermore, each possesses the "ten suchnesses," totaling one thousand suchnesses. Additionally, there are one thousand provisional names, one thousand primary retributions (*samyag-vipāka*), and one thousand environmental retributions (*niśraya-vipāka*), together forming three thousand.
Moreover, there are the three thousand inherent in principle (*li*) and the three thousand manifested in phenomena (*shi*).
The two layers of three thousand [realms] coexist within a single thought; therefore, it is called "inherent nature" (*xingju*). This concludes the clarification of inherent nature.
The above concludes the analysis of the three virtues.
II. The Harmonious Integration of the Three Virtues.
To facilitate easy understanding, these three kinds of distinctions are made. To grasp the essential meaning: the "nature as it is" (*xingju*) is the essence and the measure of the nature.

The essence of the nature is free from faults and transcends all that is non-existent; this means that the ten realms inherent in the nature are likewise free from faults and transcend all that is non-existent.
The essence of the nature is firm, solid, pure, and unstained; it is neither arising nor ceasing, eternally abiding and indestructible. The ten realms inherent in the nature are also thus. Nature...

Their measurement extends vertically to the limits of existence and horizontally throughout all realms; they are inexhaustible and inexhaustible, immeasurable and immeasurable. The same applies to the ten realms inherently possessed by nature.

As for the five aggregates of the primary retribution, their nature is identical to the substance and the measure of the Dharma-nature, being pure and all-pervasive; the same is true for the lands of the secondary retribution.

"Integration" (*rong*) means "harmony. It refers to the harmonious unification of the three virtues. This is explained in two parts: first, the unification of provisional names; second, the analogy of the primary and secondary [the Dharma-body and its environment].
The first part is further divided into two: first, the general; second, the specific. These three types of distinctions are made so that the meaning may be easily understood.

To speak in terms of grasping the essential meaning, the inherent nature (*xingju*) is itself the substance of nature (*xingti*) and the measure of nature (*xingliang*). This constitutes the general integration.

Below is a separate section, which is further divided into two parts: first, the fusion of the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and its endowment; second, the fusion of the measure (*pramāṇa*) and its endowment. The text states:

"The essential nature is free from faults and transcends non-existence. That the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are inherently endowed and free from faults and transcendent of non-existence" refers to all phenomena within the *dharmadhātu* of manifest reality.
Whether one picks up a single incense stick, a single flower, or even a single atom— *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)*
The mustard seed is entirely the essence of nature; it is entirely free from the four propositions and entirely transcends the hundred negations.

The essence of nature is firm and solid, pure and unstained, neither arising nor ceasing, eternally abiding and indestructible. That the nature is inherently endowed with the ten realms is likewise so.
This reveals that every single incense offering or flower, down to even a mote of dust or a mustard seed, is none other than the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This constitutes the fusion and realization of the inherent nature (*tixu*). Next follows the fusion and realization of the inherent capacity (*liangxu*):

the capacity of the nature is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, infinitely infinite and immeasurably immeasurable. That the ten realms are likewise inherently possessed by the nature is, accordingly—
To offer a single incense stick or a single flower is to manifest that which is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, infinite and immeasurable.

This sufficiently reveals the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena (śaśva-asaṅga-dharmadhātu). Having concluded this synthesis of provisional designations, the following provides an analogy to clarify the relationship between the primary and secondary rewards.

It responds through strategic planning. Were it otherwise, how would this differ from the supernatural powers produced by mental effort (manasikāra) in the Hīnayāna or external paths?

Regarding the "interfusion of the environment and the body" (*niśraya-pratisthā*) at the stage of fruition, where matter and mind are non-dual: the stage of fruition refers to the fruit of wondrous enlightenment, namely the final moment of mind (*paścima-citta*).

Because they are non-dual, the environment and its inhabitants are interfused; because body and land are of one suchness, form and mind are non-dual.
Regarding "manifesting forms within the nine realms to expediently deliver sentient beings": "fang" (方) means *dharma*, and "bian" (便) means *function*.

This refers to the Buddha manifesting the forms of the ten realms within the nine dharma-realms, and further employing the sixteen gates of the four teachings—making sixty-four [gates] in total—to deliver sentient beings.
The *siddhānta* (established doctrine) and skillful means lead the sentient beings of the nine realms to collectively realize the principle of the true nature (*dharmatā*).

This is entirely due to realizing that which is inherent within the causal mind; by thus realizing it, one fully realizes the principle of the three truths inherent within the causal mind of the ten realms.

By realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one attains the characteristic of *prajñā*; by realizing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one attains the function of liberation (*vimukti*); and by realizing the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*)...
Thus, one attains the essence of the Dharma-body. Therefore, the Great Master Jingxi said: "The fruition stage of all Buddhas is characterized by pervasive integration;

it merely realizes the fundamental nature of the principle inherent in all sentient beings. To 'establish according to the nature' and to 'respond without deliberation' means to accord with the nature of True Reality."

The provisional teachings (Tripitaka-yāna) and the shared teachings (Sambhoga-yāna) are established according to the nature of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). The distinct teachings (Pratyekabuddha-yāna) are established according to the nature of the middle truth (madhyama-satya).
The perfect teachings (Ekayāna) are established—whether applied suddenly, gradually, secretly, or indeterminately—exhaustively fulfilling what is appropriate;
there is no method that is not possible. All these are responses to sentient beings through non-intentionality; therefore, it is said: "responding without deliberation."

Regarding the supernormal powers attained through mental application (*manasikāra*): this refers to the fact that these powers only arise when one initiates a deliberate mental application. There are six types of such powers:

namely, the divine eye, the divine ear, recollection of past lives, knowledge of others' minds, the power of psychic mobility (*ṛddhi*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Second, the six stages of attainment (*ṣat-avasthā*) for both sages and ordinary beings distinguish its beginning and end.

The treatise states: Amitābha Buddha is one who has realized the fruit; he has perfected the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and other such merits. As for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are those who follow causes;

they are fully possessed of immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like afflictions (*kleśa*), they create immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like karmic bonds, and they are destined to undergo immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like cycles of birth and death in delusion.
The characteristic of awakening is like that of clouds and mud [vastly different].
As for the three bodies (*trikāya*): *Vairocana* in Sanskrit means "pervading all places. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The Dharma-body pervades all places; all sentient beings and lands, throughout the three periods of time, are entirely contained within it without exception."
Furthermore, there is no form or characteristic that can be apprehended. "Vairocana" in Sanskrit means "Universal Radiance. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"I, Vairocana, am now seated upon the lotus pedestal," and so forth. "Śākyamuni" in Sanskrit means "Able Sage of Silent Stillness.
However, these three names should not be rigidly adhered to as fixed identities, as seen in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* translated during the Jin dynasty.
"All are Vairocana. In the Tang translation, "all" are referred to as *Vairocana*. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Some are named Śākyamuni, some are named Vairocana," and so forth;
these are merely differences in Sanskrit pronunciation. Although there are three names, they originally possess no distinct essence.

Nevertheless, regarding these three bodies (*trikāya*), each may be discussed either individually or collectively. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is single, referring exclusively to the essential substance of original enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*).
The "single" *saṃbhogakāya* refers to the perfection of the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*). The "single" *nirmāṇakāya* refers to the manifestation of compassionate response.
Regarding the "double" *dharmakāya*: first, the *dharmakāya* of intrinsic purity; second, the *dharmakāya* of supreme wondrousness free from defilement. Regarding the "double" *saṃbhogakāya*:
first, the *saṃbhogakāya* of self-enjoyment, which is the ultimate fruit consisting of the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) of all Buddhas.
Virtue. Second is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) for others, which is the body with marks and signs seen by Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), as numerous as the atoms of a world-system.
Regarding the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are two types: first, the responsive manifestation body, which displays the eight aspects of enlightenment;

second, the emanation body, which suddenly appears where there was none to manifest the eight aspects. Furthermore, there are three kinds: first, the superior responsive body, which refers to those on the stages...

That which is seen is also called the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*). Second is the Body of the Inferior and Superior Response (*hīnaviśiṣṭanirmāṇakāya*), which is seen by those of the three vehicles according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇayāna*).
Third is the Inferior Response Body (*hīnanirmāṇakāya*), seen according to the Treasury Teaching (*piṭakayāna*) as the form of a sixteen-foot old bhikṣu. Fourth is the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*).
This refers to the transformation of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms: the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;
the seventh into the Wisdom of Equality; the sixth into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; and the first five into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done. Regarding the ten powers:
the first is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible, which knows the causes and conditions for the karmic retribution of all sentient beings. As [it is said]:

To perform wholesome karma and thereby obtain a pleasant retribution is called "the possible" (*sthāna*). To perform unwholesome karma while hoping for a wholesome retribution is called "the impossible" (*asthāna*).
Second is the power of knowing the knowledge of karma: it is the knowledge of all the karmic forces of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.

Third is the power of knowing the knowledge of meditative concentration: it is the knowledge of *dhyāna* and *samādhi*. Fourth is the power of knowing the knowledge of faculties: it is the knowledge of all sentient beings.
1. The power of knowing the superior, middling, and inferior faculties. 2. The power of knowing inclinations: knowing the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings.
3. The power of knowing elements: knowing the various worldly elements of all sentient beings. 4. The power of knowing the paths leading to their respective destinations:
knowing the characteristics of the destinations reached by all paths. 5. The power of recollecting past lives: knowing the past.
One’s lifetimes from one up to hundreds of thousands of millions, as well as one’s name, suffering and happiness, longevity and early death, and so forth.
Ninth is the power of knowledge of the divine eye, by which one sees all sentient beings at the time of their birth and death, and their rebirth in good or evil realms, and so forth.

Tenth is the power of knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, by which one knows for oneself: "My births are ended; I shall not undergo further existence. Regarding the four fearlessnesses, the first is:
First is the fearlessness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*). This means that because one has fully known and fully seen all phenomena (*dharma*), there is nothing to be feared.

Second is the fearlessness of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*). This means that because the Buddha has reached the ultimate end of the five stages of dwelling and the two types of death have forever ceased, there is nothing to be feared.

Third is the fearlessness in proclaiming the obstacles to the path (*āntarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*). This means that regarding the factors that obstruct the path, he is able to know and proclaim them; therefore, he is fearless.

Fourth is the fearlessness in proclaiming the path leading to the exhaustion of suffering (*duḥkha-kṣaya-gāminī-pratipad-vaiśāradya*). This means that regarding the path that exhausts suffering, he is able to know and proclaim it; therefore, he is fearless.
