seventh, no decline in aspiration; eighth, no decline in mindfulness; ninth, no decline in diligence; tenth, no decline in wisdom.
There is no decrease. Eleventh, there is no decrease in liberation. Twelfth, there is no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thirteenth, bodily action accords with wisdom. Fourteenth, verbal action accords with wisdom.
Fifteenth, mental action accords with wisdom. Sixteenth, he knows the past without obstruction. Seventeenth...
"Knowing the present world without obstruction" is the eighteenth [attribute]: knowing the future world without obstruction. "Virtue" (guṇa) refers to functional power.
"Ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana) refers to those who rely on others; this means the ordinary and external ordinary persons within the four teachings.

"Relying on others" applies generally to all up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), as they are all termed persons relying on others. "Possessing immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like afflictions" refers to the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāvanā-kleśa).
Regarding "afflictions," "sands-of-the-Ganges afflictions," and "ignorance afflictions":

as for "the bonds of karma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," this refers to contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karma*), uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*), and karma that is both contaminated and uncontaminated. Because the creation of karma inevitably brings about bitter fruit, it is called a "bond."

"Sands of the Ganges" births and deaths refers to the two types of birth and death: *paricchinna* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative). When karma is abundant, births and deaths are likewise many.
"Delusion and awakening" refers to the two types of delusion and awakening within the True [Nature]. To compare them to clouds and mud is to illustrate their vast disparity, like heaven and earth.
Thus, the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas is ultimately determined by delusion and awakening.
Second, regarding how delusion and awakening both rely upon the nature of the mind, yet are ultimately non-dual:
if one speaks according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are two though not two; if one discusses them according to their essence (*svabhāva*), they are not-two though two.
This is because Buddhas are the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings whom they have awakened to, while sentient beings are...

Sentient beings within the minds of all Buddhas are deluded; those who awaken do so by awakening to the nature-body (*dharmakāya*), the nature-quantity (*dharmatā-pramāṇa*), and the inherent qualities (*dharmatā-sampad*) that sentient beings fundamentally possess.
Those who are deluded do so because they are deluded regarding the nature-body, the nature-quantity, and the inherent qualities realized by all Buddhas.
Regarding what is said "according to characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), this refers to speaking in terms of the phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

"Two yet not two" means that because the cultivated virtues (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) differ, they appear as six while remaining identical; though six, they are eternally one. Regarding what is discussed "in terms of nature" (*dhātu*), this refers to speaking in terms of the rational nature (*dharmatā*) within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Two yet not two" means that because the essence of the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is one, though six, they are eternally one.
This refers to "self-identity. The passage beginning with "The Buddhas" clarifies the reason why there is non-duality. "The Buddhas" refers to the Buddhas of the four teachings:

the Dharma-body, Reward-body, Response-body, and Transformation-body. "Awakening to the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings" means that the Dharma-Buddha is the Buddha of the essential nature within the minds of sentient beings, and the Reward-Buddha is the Buddha of the inherent capacity within the minds of sentient beings.

The manifested transformation (nirmāṇakāya) is the Buddha, fully endowed with all virtues, within the minds of sentient beings. "Sentient beings" refers to those of the four teachings, namely the nine dharma-realms.
These are the sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas who are deluded; that is to say, Bodhisattvas are the sentient beings of ignorance within the minds of the Buddhas;

the followers of the Two Vehicles are the sand-like sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas; and the six classes of ordinary beings are... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
This refers to all Buddhas perceiving sentient beings within their own minds; this clarifies that [the mind] is both capable of delusion and capable of awakening.

The following section clarifies what is deluded and what is awakened. For example, it is by relying on direction that one awakens, and by relying on direction that one becomes deluded. As for the reason for awakening:

it is the awakening to the fact that sentient beings inherently possess the essence of nature (*xingti*), the measure of nature (*xingliang*), and the inherent endowment of nature (*xingju*). This means that the Dharma-Buddha awakens to the essence of nature.

The *saṃbhoga-kāya* Buddha awakens to the inherent nature (*xingju*); the *nirmāṇa-kāya* Buddha awakens to the measure of that nature (*xingliang*). Furthermore, the *dharma-kāya* Buddha attains perfect awakening; the *saṃbhoga-kāya* Buddha attains sequential awakening;

and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* Buddha attains awakening through analytical discernment. Thus, those who are deluded are deluded regarding the nature-body, the measure of the nature, and the inherent nature realized by all Buddhas.

Specifically, Bodhisattvas are deluded regarding the nature-body; the followers of the Two Vehicles are deluded regarding the inherent nature; and the six classes of ordinary beings are deluded regarding the nature.
[Measurement]. Furthermore, the six classes of ordinary beings are entirely deluded; the two vehicles are deluded regarding the conventional; and Bodhisattvas are deluded regarding the Middle Way.
Thus concludes the section on how both delusion and awakening depend upon the nature of the mind. III. The essence of the nature of the mind does not undergo delusion.
The wondrous nature of the mind—how could it be subject to delusion? To say that it is deluded yet not deluded is a statement that holds true.
Not only is it not subject to delusion, but it is also not subject to awakening. This is analogous to the fixed directions, which fundamentally possess no movement.
Delusion and enlightenment reside in the person; it is in relation to persons that there is delusion and enlightenment. Ultimately, the Dharma-nature does not belong to delusion or enlightenment.
Although it does not belong to delusion or enlightenment, it is nonetheless not separate from delusion and enlightenment. Therefore it is said: "deluded yet not deluded"—these words have their basis.
One may also say: "enlightened yet not enlightened. For the essence of the mind-nature never undergoes delusion.
○ Fourth, practice in accordance with the nature is never in vain.

Therefore, the fundamental nature-body (dharmakāya) inherently possessed by sentient beings is precisely the Dharma-body realized by all Buddhas. The measure of this nature is the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), and the inherent endowment of this nature is the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The four wisdoms, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and other such merits are all [united therein].
This can be understood through synthesis. Thus, the ancients said: "Within the minds of all Buddhas are sentient beings; in every speck of dust lies the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Within the minds of sentient beings are all Buddhas; in every thought-moment they realize the Truth. Therefore, Amitābha is my own mind, and my own mind is Amitābha.

Before a single thought is raised, one has already attained accomplishment; as soon as a thought arises, it is immediately perfected. The mutual resonance between the path and its response exists because of this.
For this reason, the merit of those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha is never in vain.

As for "the convergence can be known": the three bodies (trikāya) have already converged. Regarding the four wisdoms (caturjñāna): the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which is the essence of nature;

the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) is the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), which is the magnitude of nature; and the wisdom of accomplishing tasks (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna) is the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which is [the function of] nature.

[The text] is complete. The Wisdom of Observation (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) penetrates the three bodies (trikāya), the ten powers (daśabala), the four fearlessnesses (catvāri vaiśāradyāni), the unique qualities (āveṇikadharma), and so forth;

each of these is divided according to the four teachings (caturvidha-deśanā). By combining the four teachings with the three bodies, they may be understood. Thus, when it says "as the ancient masters have said," this is an invocation of antiquity to provide scriptural proof.
"Every dust mote is the Land of Ultimate Bliss" because sentient beings are themselves Buddhas. "In every thought-moment one realizes the Truth" because Buddhas are themselves sentient beings.
Since Buddhas are themselves sentient beings, Amitābha is my own mind. Since sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, my own mind is Amitābha.
That which is already perfected even before a single thought is raised is the virtue of one's nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
This is the fundamental nature. The moment a thought arises, it is immediately perfected; this is because cultivated virtue accords with the inherent nature.
Hence it is said: "A single thought in accord is a single Buddha; every thought in accord is a Buddha. Regarding the two phrases on the mutual resonance of response and stimulus:
I am the stimulus, and the Buddha is the object of the stimulus; the Buddha is the response, and I am the object of the response. Thus it is.

Regarding "the perfectly interfused essence of the Dharma-realm," this refers to the essence of the Dharma-realm of non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).

It is called "perfect" (*yuan*) because it penetrates vertically through time and pervades horizontally across space; it is called "interfused" (*rong*) because every phenomenon is without obstruction. That it "constitutes my single thought-moment" may also be understood as follows:
It is entirely appropriate to speak of the objects of a single thought-moment, the fragrance of a single thought-moment, the flowers of a single thought-moment, and so forth.

That which is "the whole body being the Dharma-realm" refers to the fourfold Dharma-realm: the object of contemplation is the phenomenal Dharma-realm (*shih-fa-chieh*), while the subject that contemplates is the noumenal Dharma-realm (*li-fa-chieh*).

Subject and object are non-dual; this is the Dharma-realm of the unimpeded interfusion of principle and phenomena. To be fully endowed with the three thousand [realms] is the Dharma-realm of the unimpeded interfusion of phenomena and phenomena.

The Correct Exposition. [This section has three parts: First, the formal exposition; second, the citation of evidence; third, the illustration by contrast.

Regarding the first: The treatise says: "When a practitioner recites the Buddha’s name, when they perform the visualization of the Buddha, or when they perform other visualizations such as those of the primary and attendant figures, the environment and its inhabitants, or the primary and secondary aspects of reality."
Whether one is practicing the three kinds of pure karma, abiding in single-mindedness without distraction, or invoking the Name with a distracted mind—

The whole body is itself the Dharma-realm.
As for the three kinds of pure karma: first, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, and practicing non-killing with a compassionate heart.
First, they cultivate the ten wholesome karmas. Second, they receive and uphold the Three Refuges, fully observing the various precepts and not violating the rules of dignified conduct (*vīrya*).

Third, they have deep faith in cause and effect, read and recite Mahāyāna sutras, and exhort practitioners to advance. Regarding "views and thoughts" (*dṛṣṭi-vitarka*), this refers to the two delusions of views and thoughts. "Views" refers to the five views:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), and the view of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*). "Thoughts" refers to greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt—the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Affliction" (nǎo) refers to the inexhaustibility of the afflictions (*kleśa*). The Great Outline of Chan Master Che’s Ten Gates states:

"Nevertheless, among these ten gates, the fifth gate is the most essential, for it encompasses the meanings of phenomena and principle, the general and the particular, nature and cultivation, and the horizontal and vertical."
The focus does not lie outside this single thought, for it is the entirety of the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, if a student can thoroughly clarify this one gate, then all preceding and subsequent gates are fully contained within it. I shall now briefly indicate this:
first, to show the main text itself. When a practitioner is precisely at the moment of invoking the Name, this is the very time of the visualization of becoming a Buddha; that is to say:

Single-mindedly focusing on the Great Name constitutes both the subject that contemplates and the object that is contemplated. Within this, the ten dharma-methods for perfecting the vehicle are fully present:
the Great Name being recited is the inconceivable realm; the one who recites it is the inconceivable bodhicitta;
the non-duality of subject and object is inconceivable *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; and their mutual correspondence in every thought-moment is the universal penetration of dharmas.

If one realizes this meaning, one immediately recognizes what is open and what is obstructed. When there is mindfulness, that is mindfulness; when there is an object of mindfulness, that is the foundation of mindfulness—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

To maintain mindfulness from moment to moment without allowing it to become discontinuous is right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*). If one's practice matures, these become the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Through the full maturation of such practice, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) arise. Because the faculties have arisen, their power and function increase, which are the five [powers] (*pañcabala*).
The power of moment-to-moment awakening and illumination is the seven factors of enlightenment; proceeding with peace and stability is the eightfold noble path.

When these factors of the path are harmonized, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or even when performing earnest prayers and prostrations, this constitutes the "aids to penetration" (*pratipakṣa*).

One must recognize the stages of the six levels of realization (*ṣaḍ-vidha-yoga*) and not give rise to arrogance. Without being moved by deluded thoughts, one will be able to practice patient endurance through the past.
To take birth as one's goal is to immediately depart from attachment to dharmas. This constitutes the tenfold method of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-vidhi*).

It is also applied when performing other contemplations regarding the principal and its attendants, or the primary and secondary environments; as the *Commentary on the Sutra* states: "Although there are sixteen contemplations, by speaking of the Buddha, all are encompassed;

this means that the principal includes the attendants, and the primary includes the secondary. Furthermore, it applies when practicing the three kinds of pure karma; that is to say, "I now contemplate..."
The Buddha’s instruction for those seeking rebirth is precisely for the sake of one’s past inexhaustible parents, one’s inexhaustible teachers and elders, and immeasurable sentient beings.
Within every thought-moment, one should fully possess these three minds. A single utterance of the Great Name is itself the ten wholesome deeds of the highest grade;
this is precisely the Three Refuges as a single essence. When maintained continuously from moment to moment, it is complete.
One fulfills the multitude of precepts; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one does not depart from them, thereby not violating the rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).

Taking mindfulness of the Buddha as the cause and the Pure Land as the fruit, one should properly maintain this continuity of thought moment after moment. This is precisely the Mahāyāna sūtras; it is this very mind that is the Buddha;

it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). One should likewise use this to exhort practitioners. Furthermore, even when the floods of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are vast and turbulent...
Because afflictions have never been severed, this is a brief outline of the fundamental principles. To further clarify, ten gates are established.

Since it is said that the Dharma-realm is the entire body [of reality], this constitutes the Gate of the Single True Dharma-realm. The Buddha who is the object of mindfulness is the inherent nature; the mind that performs the mindfulness is the capacity of nature;
and the non-duality of subject and object is the essence of nature. These are the Three Truths. The mindful subject belongs to the body... [the object belongs to] the realm.
Mindfulness belongs to the earth. The capacity [to remember] and the object [remembered] are one in dependent origination; this is the gate of the mutual interpenetration of body and land.

That the capacity is the object and the object is the capacity is the gate of the mutual identity of mind and land. The capacity to remember is the sentient being, and the object remembered is the Buddha;

since the capacity and the object are non-dual, this is the gate of the non-duality of sentient beings and Buddhas. The capacity to remember is the contemplation, and the object remembered is the realm; when separated from the capacity...

There is no object; being free from objects, there is no subjectivity. This is the gate of the mutual swallowing of the object and the contemplation. The object is wondrous provisionality, and the contemplation is emptiness;

the simultaneous vanishing of both object and contemplation is the Middle Way. This is the gate of the naturalness of the three contemplations. The contemplating subject is the stimulus, and the contemplated object is the response;
this is the gate of the spontaneous functioning of stimulus and response. The contemplating subject is "this," and the contemplated object is "that"; yet subject and object are not...

Second: This is the gate of the mutual identity of self and other. At the very moment one recites the Buddha’s name, it is the moment of rebirth in the Pure Land, the moment of attaining Buddhahood, and the moment of delivering sentient beings.
Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally, it is the gate of the mutual presence of the present and the future. To further explain the title:
A single utterance of the Buddha’s name perfectly encompasses the Three Bodies and Four Lands of Amitābha. Precisely at the moment of recitation, the four lands are completely purified.
One perfectly perceives the three bodies (*trikāya*), perfectly transforms the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), and perfectly realizes the three non-regressions.

Thus the text says: "By means of this wondrous mind, one recollects that Amitābha; then which of his three bodies would not be recollected? Seeking those four lands (*catasraḥ bhūmayaḥ*), which land would not be born into? This explains the Pure Land:
a single utterance of the Buddha’s name is the great dependent origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*) of the Buddha-realm. The Buddha-realm...

Once it has arisen, the nine [aspects] are likewise manifested; this is the teaching of dependent origination. A single utterance of the Buddha’s name is the entirety of the Buddha as one’s own mind—this is the school of "Mind-only.

Both mind and Buddha—this is the school of "perfect interfusion. To be without thought or discrimination is...
The school that transcends emotion and leaves behind views clarifies its fundamental tenet: the moment one recites the Buddha’s name is the moment one attains Buddhahood.

This naturally surpasses the provisional benefits of the Three Vehicles, thereby manifesting the supreme benefit. At the very moment of recitation, the whole body is birth; yet, as it is solely this One Mind, there is no birth.
Being neither mind nor Buddha, it is neither birth nor non-birth. Thus, mind and Buddha are distinct and clear...

Thus, it is both arising and non-arising. It perfectly encompasses the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and yet perfectly transcends them. Furthermore, at the very moment it perfectly encompasses them, it perfectly transcends them;

at the very moment it perfectly transcends them, it perfectly encompasses them. This perfect encompassing and perfect transcending are simultaneous and unimpeded—this is the discourse on arising and non-arising.
The explanation of the title is hereby concluded. When reciting the name of the Buddha, one should act in this manner.
The Buddha contemplates the times; even down to the vast expanse of views and thoughts, there is nothing that is not thus. In the slightest movement of the mind, the Three Truths are fully present;
therefore, this is the entire substance of the Dharma-realm. The formal exposition is concluded.

"Other minds" refers to the minds of afflictions such as *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*. If even the minds of sentient beings are still [the Way], how much more so the mind of the Buddha! This is the correct [interpretation].

These merely correspond to the depth or shallowness of one's meritorious practice and the high or low level of one's stage of attainment.
The preceding passage explained the principle within phenomena; that principle is fundamentally perfect and subtle. This, however, demonstrates the phenomena within the principle. As for phenomena—

There are distinctions of gradation. Since the principle is fundamentally perfect and subtle, the six stages are eternally identical [to the ultimate]. Since phenomena possess gradations, that which is identical is eternally sixfold.

Therefore, one must distinguish the meaning of the "six identities" (*liuji*). If one’s practice reaches the stage of "practice through contemplation" (*guanxingwei*), one will be born in the Land of Peaceful Coexistence (*tongju jingtu*), where there are three grades and nine ranks.
Because the delusions common to the two realms have not yet been severed, one beholds the response-body of Amitābha.

The Treatise says: That the objective realm and contemplation mutually encompass one another is precisely due to the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (shishi wuai).
The reason why phenomena and phenomena are without obstruction is what is meant by "that which has its source is thus."

Regarding "the fundamental basis" (*youben*): this refers to the subsequent section which clarifies that very basis. For now, we first clarify the contemplation of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai guan*).
Master Ouyi’s commentary on the verse for visualizing the offering states: "The nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and still;
the resonance of their mutual response is inconceivable. These six lines, beginning with "My place of practice is like the jewels of Indra," clarify their mutual interpenetration.
Universally and mutually endowed with wondrous contemplation, this profoundly reveals the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).

First, as for the one who performs the prostration, it consists of my own three karmas: namely, the body-karma of diligent exertion, the speech-karma of single-minded devotion, and the mind-karma of reverence.

These three are all dharmas produced by causes and conditions; whatever belongs to dependent origination is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature. That is to say, they do not arise from themselves, from another, or from both.
Because they are free [from intrinsic nature], their nature is empty and quiescent; by virtue of being empty and quiescent, they are able to manifest as responsive.

Thus, they respond within quiescence, and remain quiescent even while responding; therefore, they are difficult to conceive. Those who are venerated are the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth—the three bodies (*trikāya*).

These three are all phenomena produced by causes and conditions; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty and quiescent. Because they are empty and quiescent, they are able to manifest as responsive.
It is quiescent yet responsive; it is responsive yet remains quiescent. Therefore, it is difficult to conceive. It is like two mirrors reflecting one another:
because they are bright and pure, they are able to manifest each other's images. Each acts as the illuminator and each acts as the illuminated. Thus, the way of resonance and response intersects.
It is also thus. Although the reflections within two mirrors are each layered and infinite, they neither enter nor exit, nor do they come or go.
Such is the original nature of the *dharmatā*; how could it be conceived?

Having realized this inconceivable *dharmatā*, one then knows that my single room, the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), is fundamentally equal to the *dharmadhātu* and the realm of empty space throughout the ten directions.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time all appear vividly within this single room, just as a *cintāmaṇi* jewel universally manifests all things.

Furthermore, one knows that the ocean-like assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions and three periods of time are likewise entirely so, just as a *cintāmaṇi* jewel universally manifests all things. Therefore, although my body is here, it is certain...
In meditative concentration, one universally manifests one’s reflection before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

This means that it is not merely a single body prostrating to a single Buddha; rather, a single body universally prostrates to all Buddhas, and furthermore, all bodies mutually prostrate to all Buddhas.
These are mutually pervasive in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), and mutually complete in accordance with the nature. Such an inexhaustible cloud of bodies—people...

Humanity is inherently endowed [with this nature]; it does not depend upon deliberate arrangement to become so. As it is with the cloud-bodies of myself, so too are the cloud-bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Since this is the case for the primary retribution (*samyag-vipāka*), it is likewise so for the secondary environment (*niśraya-vipāka*). Therefore, this constitutes the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
The section on "The Manifestation of the Source" is concluded.

This is because the inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused *dharmadhātu* constitutes my single thought-moment;

The Dharma-realm. Therefore it is said: "A single atom is not small as the Dharma-realm; the ocean of lands is not large as the Dharma-realm.
Much is the Dharma-realm, and little is the Dharma-realm.
"By" (*you*) refers to the cause; "resulting in" (*zhi*) refers to the logical principle. That every phenomenon is unimpeded is because of this Dharma.

The inconceivable interpenetration of the realms (*dhātu*) is not something that can be fathomed by intellectual reasoning. That which is the inconceivable essence of interpenetration is precisely the one true *dharmadhātu*.
The non-obstruction between phenomena (*śaśva-arvāg-asaṅga*) arises because the nature-inherent [reality] is identical to the essence and the magnitude of that nature.
To take "my single thought-moment" as the subject refers to the entire body of the *dharmadhātu* being taken as my single thought-moment, the capacity for cultivation.
The mind-dharma is not merely a small portion of the dharma-realm; since this mind is the entire body of the dharma-realm, it is thus vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive.

Furthermore, when it is said that the entire substance acts as the sentient being, the Buddha, the support, and the primary object, this too refers to the entire body of the dharma-realm acting as the sentient beings, dharmas, Buddha-dharmas, supporting dharmas, and primary dharmas to be contemplated—nor is it a mere small portion of the dharma-realm.
[This applies] even down to a single speck of dust or a single mustard seed; it is thus for every phenomenon (*dharma*).

Since all things are manifested as the total embodiment [of reality], what single phenomenon is there that does not vertically exhaust the past and future and horizontally pervade all space? Therefore, it is said: "A single speck of dust is no small *dharmadhātu*; an ocean of lands is no large *dharmadhātu*.
Because the *dharmadhātu* has neither smallness nor largeness, the many are the *dharmadhātu*, and the few are also the *dharmadhātu*. The *dharmadhātu*..."

Because there is neither more nor less, and because each phenomenon (dharma) is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive without mutual obstruction, it is therefore called the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
This concludes the clarification of the underlying causes and conditions.

Therefore, the sixteen objective realms of the Western [Pure Land] and my own two contemplations of phenomena and principle are, one by one, none other than the entire body of the Dharma-realm.
It is like the net of Indra within the palace of Śakra; although each individual jewel is distinct from the others, their reflections...

Entering into the various jewels: although their reflections enter the various jewels, the functions of their illumination toward the east and west remain distinct. The relationship between object (*viṣaya*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is likewise.

If one takes the object as the phenomenal (*sāṃvṛtika*), then contemplation is the principle (*tattva*); since the principle can encompass phenomena, this is called "contemplation swallowing the object.

If one takes contemplation as the phenomenal, then the object is the principle; since the principle can encompass phenomena, this is called "the object swallowing contemplation. Whether it be contemplation or the object, or...
One is the phenomenon (dharma) and the others are the principle (li); or one is the principle and the others are the phenomena. As these mutually encompass one another, they are like Indra’s net.

The text is divided into three sections: first, the clarification of the principle of perfect interfusion; second, the citation of metaphors for perfect interfusion; and third, the application of the contemplation of perfect interfusion.

The phrase "Thus" (*yǐshì*)承接 (承接) the preceding textual meaning.
Furthermore, among the sixteen realms, there is not one that is not the entire manifestation of the Dharma-realm; all objects of contemplation are the very substance and magnitude of the nature.

Through this mutual pervasion and mutual containment, they are able to swallow one another—each acting as both the devourer and the devoured—in an infinitely layered manner, thereby constituting the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*). This serves as the basis for...
Contemplation. Thus, the preceding text speaks of the wondrous contemplation of mutual pervasion and mutual inclusion, saying: "It is like two mirrors reflecting one another;

The realms, such as the realm of empty space, and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and three periods of time, are all vividly manifested within this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), just as the jewels of Indra universally manifest all things. The essence of this Dharma-realm is profoundly still and pure, beyond all comparison; it is merely illustrated by the metaphor of the imperial jewel (*maṇi*).
Within this metaphor, the fourfold Dharma-realm is complete: the substance of the jewel represents the phenomenal Dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*), for each individual jewel is distinct from the others;

The Dharma-realm of non-obstruction: reflections and reflections are all vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, infinitely layered and inexhaustible; this is a metaphor for the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.
The *Fanwang jing hezhu* (Combined Commentary on the Brahma Net Sutra) states: "The reflection of one pearl appears in all pearls;

Regarding the distinction between illumination and function: "one bead abides in the position of each individual bead" refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

"The same applies to contemplation" refers to the harmonious fusion of wondrous contemplation. "Taking the realm as the phenomenal" means taking the objective realm that is being contemplated as the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
It is like a reflection within a pearl. To take contemplation as the principle means that the wisdom which contemplates is the principle-dharmadhātu, like the luster of the pearl.
That the principle can encompass phenomena is like the luster being able to contain the reflection; this is what is meant by "contemplation swallowing the object."
This refers to the following passage: "The environment and its inhabitants of the Western [Pure Land] are already within the scope of my contemplation.
Regarding "taking contemplation as the phenomenon," this means taking the contemplating wisdom as the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), like the reflection in a pearl.

Regarding "taking the object as the principle," this means taking the contemplated object as the noumenal dharma-realm, like the radiance of the pearl. That the principle can encompass the phenomenon is like how radiance can contain reflections.
This is what is meant by "the object swallowing the contemplation. As the subsequent text states: "My present body and mind are now within the realm of the dependent and the primary.

If one considers either the contemplation or the object, or takes them as a single entity, this means that both the contemplating subject and the contemplated object together constitute the phenomenal dharma-realm (shih-fa-chieh), like a shadow.
The rest are the noumenal [dharma-realm] (li): the remaining fifteen objects constitute the noumenal dharma-realm (li-fa-chieh), like light."

Furthermore, principle (*li*) can encompass phenomena (*shi*). Just as the light from each individual jewel contains all reflections, or when one [jewel] is taken as principle—the subject that observes and the object observed—then the single totality constitutes the Dharma-realm of Principle (*li-fajie*), like the light;

while the remaining fifteen objects constitute the Dharma-realm of Phenomena (*shi-fajie*), like the reflections. Thus, principle can encompass phenomena, just as the light of a single jewel contains all reflections. This applies to both cases.

"Mutually swallowing one another" reveals the inexhaustible depth of layers, wherein they mutually pervade and mutually contain; this is the wondrous contemplation of the non-obstruction between phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*).
The formal discussion of mutual swallowing is hereby concluded.
II. Concluding Indication of the Pure Land School:
If this is so, then when I practice contemplation, the Western Land’s environment and its inhabitants are already within the scope of my contemplation;
and my current body and mind are already within that environment and its inhabitants. To seek birth in An-yang (Sukhāvatī) with such realization may be called "a wild goose passing through the sky."
The vast sky: its reflection sinks into the cold water; the wild geese have lost all trace of their passage, and the water has no intention of retaining their image.
This concludes the meaning of the Pure Land school’s "arising from non-arising" and "non-arising arising.

When it says "at the time I practice contemplation," it refers precisely to the time one is cultivating the visualization. By analogy, this applies to ritual prostrations, repentance, offerings, reading sutras, reciting the Buddha’s name, and the dedication of merit.
When making vows, practicing seated meditation, and so forth, it is thus with pure karma; even when performing evil karma, it is no different.
This place of my practice is like a *cintāmaṇi* jewel: the environments and beings of the Western Land are already within the scope of my contemplation.
The environments and beings of the Western Land are likewise like a *cintāmaṇi* jewel: my current body, mind, and all karmic actions are already within those environments and beings.
Within this, such is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

Because it is only at the time of practicing contemplation that one first illuminates and realizes it, if one understands this meaning, one will know that birth is indeed birth, yet birth is non-birth; departure is truly no departure, yet no departure is departure.
Furthermore, by analogy, one should know that Amitābha’s reception is indeed reception, yet reception is non-reception; coming...
Thus, in reality, there is no coming. This is the meaning of "coming without coming. Therefore, Master Tiānyī Huái addressed the assembly, saying:
"In the Zen school, it is said 'no-birth' (wu-sheng); in the Pure Land school, it is said 'birth' (you-sheng). Is it birth, or is it no-birth? It is said:
'If born, one is certainly born; yet in going, one truly does not go. It is like a wild goose passing through the sky."
The vast sky; shadows sink into the cold water. The wild geese have severed the intent to leave a trace; the water lacks the mind to retain the shadow.

When the geese pass through the vast sky, their shadows sink into the cold water. This is a metaphor for birth: one who is born is certain to be born. The geese have severed their intent; the water has no mind.
The absence of any sign of coming or going in the interim illustrates that although there is movement, in reality there is no going.

Furthermore, the meaning of the wild geese leaving no tracks illustrates non-arising; yet, since tracks are nonetheless left behind, this illustrates that while there is no arising, arising occurs spontaneously.

Water has no intention to retain a reflection; this is a metaphor for the Buddha not coming to receive one. Yet, that the reflection remains of its own accord is a metaphor for being received spontaneously despite not being formally received.

Such is the effortless, natural operation of the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion; it is not a supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) produced through deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*).
The section on "The Gate of the Mutual Absorption of Object and Contemplation" concludes.
Section 7: The Gate of the Three Contemplations as the Natural Order (Dharmatā). Part Two. First, the verse; second, the prose commentary. Now, the first:

The contemplating subject constitutes the three contemplations, and the contemplated object consists of the three truths. Because cultivation arises entirely from within the intrinsic nature (dharmatā), it is termed the "natural order."

To be able to contemplate [reality] as the three contemplations means that the entire nature-body, nature-quantity, and nature-endowment—the inherent virtues of the three truths—arise to constitute the cultivated virtues of the three contemplations;
and these cultivated virtues of the three contemplations, in turn, illuminate the inherent virtues of the three truths.

Therefore it is said: "Cultivation arises from the fullness of nature; cultivation is fully present within nature. Regarding the non-duality of nature and cultivation, the *Great Meaning of Stopping and Contemplation* states:

"The three truths and the three contemplations are neither three nor not-three; three, one, and one are three, yet have no locus. The names 'truth' and 'contemplation' differ, but their substance is identical.
Thus, the duality of subject and object is not two; therefore, it is called 'dharmatā' (the natural state of phenomena)."

II. The Section on the Treatise is divided into two parts: first, the explicit exposition of the three contemplations; second, the concluding indication of the Pure Land school. The first part is further divided into two:

first, the individual discussion; second, the general discussion. The first of these is further divided into two: first, the simultaneous presentation of the truths and the contemplations; second, the individual discussion of the truths and the contemplations. Now, the first [of these].
The Treatise says: The "three truths" are the True, the Conventional, and the Middle. The "three contemplations" are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
As for "truth" (*satya*), it means to investigate with precision. That is to say, to investigate all phenomena with precision, they are precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
Emptiness is the true truth of the nature’s capacity; the provisional is the conventional truth of the nature’s inherent endowment; and the middle is the middle truth of the nature’s essence.
These three distinct [aspects] are the successive three truths; these three and one in perfect fusion are the perfectly fused three truths.

"Contemplation" (guan) has the meaning of illuminating and realizing. Illuminating the True [Truth] is the contemplation of emptiness; illuminating the Conventional is the contemplation of the provisional; illuminating the Middle is the contemplation of the middle.
These three distinct [contemplations] are the successive three contemplations; these three and one without obstruction are the perfectly fused three contemplations.
The general exposition of the contemplation of the truths is concluded. II.
The specific exposition of the contemplation of the truths has two parts: first, the specific exposition of the intrinsic virtue (*dharmatā-guṇa*) of the three truths;

second, the specific exposition of the cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) of the three contemplations. The first part has three sections: first, a precise discussion of the three truths; second, their convergence into the one mind; third, the conclusion.
The Accomplishment of the Virtues of Nature. First, regarding the initial section:

In forgetting emotions and severing conceptual understanding, nothing is more supreme than the True (zhen); in responding to conditions through application, nothing is more supreme than the Conventional (su). These two are harmoniously integrated within emptiness and existence.
Nothing is more supreme than the Middle Way.
"True" refers to true emptiness, which means the total dissolution of all phenomena. For all phenomena are fundamentally empty;

yet sentient beings do not understand this, grasping at them as real and thereby giving rise to deluded views. If one uses the contemplation of emptiness to wash away these [views], then that which was called "real" [is seen for what it is].
Sentimental understanding is naturally forgotten; thus it is said that "sentiments are forgotten and understanding is severed. Nothing is more supreme than the Real.

"The mundane" refers to the secular world, which is the designation for the establishment of all phenomena (*dharma*). Although all phenomena are fundamentally empty, if one contemplates them through the perspective of the provisional (*prajñā*), [they appear as such].
Thus, one is able to clearly and thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are inherently complete within the nature, appearing vividly and distinctly.

Therefore, it is said that in the application of responding to conditions according to circumstances, nothing surpasses the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). "Middle" (*madhya*) refers to the central correctness, which signifies the unification of all phenomena.

All phenomena are originally neither identical to nor separate from the two extremes; if one observes them through the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), then one is able to clearly and thoroughly comprehend all phenomena.
Dharma is neither real nor conventional; it is both real and conventional. It is perfectly interfused and unimpeded: three in one, and one in three—beyond conceptual thought.
Therefore, it is said that the integration of emptiness and existence is nothing more exalted than the Middle Way. This concludes the detailed discussion of the Three Truths.
Second, these two ultimately converge in the one mind.
Its vacuity and spirit are unobscured; this is the inherent emptiness of my own mind. When objects arrive, it responds; this is the inherent existence of my own mind.
Emptiness and existence are mutually identical; this is the inherent centrality of my own mind.

That which is empty yet lucid and never obscured is that which, while responding to conditions, remains eternally unchanging. That which responds as things arrive is that which, while remaining unchanging, eternally follows conditions.
That emptiness and existence are mutually identical means that it is precisely while following conditions that it is unchanging, and precisely while being unchanging that it follows conditions.
Thus, all is ultimately resolved within the One Mind.
Third, the establishment of the nature of the virtues of the essence (*dharmatā-guṇa*). This is the essence; it is not cultivation. It is the three truths; it is not three. It is contemplation.
This concludes the separate discussion on the nature of the virtues of the three truths.

II. A detailed discussion of the cultivation of merit through the three contemplations has three parts: first, the differentiation of their characteristics; second, the manifestation of their perfect fusion;
third, the conclusion establishing the cultivated merit. Now, the first part.

One who cultivates this practice illuminates and realizes it in accordance with its true nature. Thus, to realize that this mind is empty and devoid of any substantial entity is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā).

To illuminate and realize that this nature is fully endowed with all phenomena is called "provisionality" (prajñapti). To harmonize these two extremes as being neither identical nor different is called the "Middle Way" (madhyamā-pratipad).
"To cultivate it" refers to the manifestation of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) as distinct from inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

"Illuminating through accordance with nature" means that the merit of cultivated virtue accords with the principle of inherent virtue. "Embodiment and penetration of this mind" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-darśana*).

Because one embodies and penetrates this mind that functions in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartin*), it is never altered by external objects; hence it is said to be "vast, empty, and non-existent."
Things are called "emptiness. To clearly illuminate this nature is the "wondrous provisional contemplation" (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).

This means that while clearly illuminating this unchanging nature, it constantly accords with the conditions of the myriad phenomena; therefore, it is said to be "fully endowed with the myriad phenomena," which is termed "the provisional."

"Integrating the two extremes" refers to the contemplation of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong guan*). Nature is the essence (*ti*), while mind is the function (*yong*); therefore, they are not identical.
Since there is no function apart from essence, and no essence apart from function, they are not different. Thus, it is said that "neither identical nor different" is what is meant by the "Middle Way.
This concludes the analysis of the characteristics of practice.
II. Manifesting Perfect Interfusion.

Thus, it is precisely within emptiness and spirit that one responds to phenomena; it is precisely in responding to phenomena that one is empty and spiritual. Emptiness is precisely the provisional and the middle.
The provisional is precisely emptiness and the middle. The middle is precisely emptiness and the provisional.
"However, this is to say... refers back to the preceding text. The three contemplations are but a single mind; therefore, they are said to be mutually identical.
That which is empty and lucid yet responds to objects is the essence being the function. That which responds to objects yet remains empty and lucid is... [the function being the essence].
This is precisely that very substance. Substance and function are nothing other than the one mind; therefore, it is said that the three contemplations are mutually identical.
This concludes the demonstration of perfect interfusion. III. Concluding with the Formation of Cultivated Virtue.
This is cultivation in accordance with the nature of reality; it is illumination that transcends all dependencies; it is the inconceivable threefold contemplation;
it is the compass for the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama. Such is the specific discussion.
To cultivate in accordance with the nature means that nature and cultivation are non-dual. To illuminate by transcending all dependencies means that subject and object are non-dual.
The inconceivable threefold contemplation means that the three contemplations are non-dual. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the compass for guidance, means that cause and effect are non-dual.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *Śūraṅgama*; here it is translated as "Ultimate Solidity. This is the fruit.

"Awakening" is another name for it. "The South Pointer" refers to the compass needle pointing south. Because the threefold contemplation within a single mind is the cause of Great Samādhi, it is called the "South Pointer.
This concludes the separate discussion.
II. General Discussion of the Two [Truths]. First, the differentiation of their characteristics; second, the manifestation of their perfect interfusion. Now, for the first:

if one discusses them generally, one may take the void and numinous nature of our own mind as emptiness (śūnyatā), the myriad phenomena that are observed as the provisional (prajñapti), and the non-duality of mind and objects as the middle (madhyama).

The preceding passage was specific, discussing the contemplation of the mind in particular; the present passage is general, synthesizing both the mind and its objects as being of a single nature alone.
Because the nature of the mind is without marks, it is emptiness; because it transforms into all phenomena, it is the provisional.
Since the mind is identical to the object and the object is identical to the mind, they are non-dual, which is the Middle Way. This concludes the analysis of their modes of activity.
II. Manifesting Perfect Interfusion: Objects are the objects of my own mind;
how could they be provisional without being empty? The mind is the mind of all things; how could it be empty without being provisional?

Mind is identical to objects, and objects are identical to mind. How could there be a middle that is not both empty and provisional? (It must be that this very emptiness and provisionality is the middle.)
"Things are the things of my own mind; what is not empty by virtue of being provisional? This refers to the objects of observation, which are objects manifested by the nature of the mind.

How could they not be empty, given that they are neither provisional nor central [to a separate reality], but are instead identical to the inherent nature and the substance of that nature, which is the measure of the nature itself?
"The mind is the mind of all things; what is empty that is not provisional? This refers to the observing mind.
This is the mind capable of transformation through objective conditions (*ālambana*). What is empty and what is the Middle Way that is not itself the Provisional?

It is because the nature-quantity and the nature-substance are inherently possessed; mind is identical to things, and things are identical to mind. What is empty and provisional that is not identical to the Middle?
This means that the nature of the mind and the nature of objects are but a single nature. Therefore it is said: "What is empty and what is provisional that is not [the Middle]?"

This is precisely the Middle [Truth]. Thus, that which is the inherent nature, capacity, and endowment is the essence of nature itself. This concludes the formal explanation of the Three Contemplations.
Second, the summary and demonstration of the Pure Land school:
Therefore, as for contemplating the environment and inhabitants of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one uses the three contemplations of one's own single mind to contemplate that single object.

Regarding the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), there is nothing that is not possible. To employ the single mind of my threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) to illumine the single realm of those three truths—this, too, is entirely possible.
Master Huxi said: "The realm is wondrous conventionality (*prajñapti-satya*); the contemplation is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

When both realm and contemplation are forgotten, this is the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). How could forgetting and illumination ever have a sequence? Within the single mind, all is fused and severed, leaving no trace. What more is there to say?"
Is it not the case that the method of the three contemplations is thus?
To contemplate the three truths of that single object by means of the three contemplations of my own single mind is what constitutes rational contemplation (*li-guan*).
This is also a distinct contemplation. To employ one mind of my threefold contemplation to illuminate that single object of the three truths is the contemplation of phenomena;
it is also a comprehensive contemplation, and it is precisely the exclusive invocation of the Name. Such is this Pure Land school.
It depends solely upon making the vow to seek birth [in that realm]. Therefore, whether one practices general contemplation or specific contemplation, there is nothing that is not permissible.
The Great Master Huxi—namely, Dharma Master Huaize of the Yuan Dynasty—composed the *Verses on the Three Contemplations of One Mind*, which state:

"The object is wondrous conventionality (*miao-ja*)," and so forth. That "the object is wondrous conventionality" is precisely the mind. That "contemplation is emptiness (*kong*)" is precisely the object.

Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous extinction of both object and contemplation: this means neither mind nor object. As for the extinction and illumination, how could there ever be a sequence between them?
They are simultaneous. When the single mind is fused and severed, leaving no trace whatsoever, it is simply the wondrous mind of the Middle Way.
Furthermore, there are no traces of emptiness or the provisional. Since the three contemplations are fully present within daily activity, how could anything not be suchness?
The section on the gate of the three contemplations as the natural order of reality concludes.
Section Eight: The Gate of Spontaneous Response and Resonance. Part One: The Verse. Part Two: The Treatise.
Now, the first [the verse]: My mind invokes the Buddhas; Amitābha responds from afar. The nature of Heaven spontaneously connects them, like a magnet attracting a needle.
Regarding the signs of resonance (*ganying*), four propositions are briefly clarified. First is "mysterious resonance and mysterious response.

This refers to having cultivated the three karmas well in the past, yet not yet having deployed body or speech in the present; it is through the power of past goodness that this constitutes mysterious resonance.
Although no spiritual omens are currently perceived, one is secretly benefited by the *dharmakāya*. Though neither seen nor heard, one awakens to and knows [this benefit]. This is...

having planted roots of goodness in the past, they become a hidden stimulus that has reached fruition, whereby one immediately encounters a Buddha and hears the Dharma, obtaining benefit in the present life; this is called a manifest response. For example, when a Buddha first appears in the world...

Regarding those who were first to attain deliverance: how could they have ever practiced in the present? It is precisely this principle that the Tathāgata, perceiving their past capacities (*pūrvakarmendriya*), went of his own accord to deliver them.

Yet one can still evoke a descent [of the sacred]. For example, when Sudatta knelt for a long time, the Buddha went to the Jeta Grove. Or again, as in the repentance rituals at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one can evoke spiritual portents;
this refers to an evident evocation resulting in an evident response. Fourth, regarding an evident evocation resulting in a hidden response:

it is like a person who, throughout their life, has diligently practiced and accumulated abundant merit through good deeds, yet no evident response appears, while a hidden benefit nonetheless exists. This is an evident evocation resulting in a hidden [response].
It is so. If one understands these four intentions, then all acts of lowering the head or raising the hand will be known not to result in the vain abandonment of merit;
throughout the day there will be no cause for regret. If one sees those who take pleasure in killing long-lived beings or who delight in giving to the poor, one should not give rise to false views.
To discuss this in detail, there are thirty-six propositions and various other meanings. This is the nature of Heaven.
"Those [who possess it]" refers to the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). "Related" means connected. There are two kinds of connection: namely, natural affinity (*dharmatā*) and vow (*praṇidhāna*).
I have only a connection of natural affinity with all Buddhas; however, regarding Amitābha, I possess both kinds.
Therefore, I have the most profound affinity (*sambandha*) with Amitābha. As for the magnet: it is a stone that attracts iron, produced on the sunny side of a mountain.
Iron. In the mountains of Shanyin, there must necessarily be lodestone. This is because these two substances share the same fundamental nature (*dhātu*).

The second section, the Treatise on the Discourse, is divided into three parts: first, the correlation of innate nature; second, the correlation of vows; third, the conclusion indicating the Pure Land school.
Now, the first part.
The Treatise says: All Buddhas and sentient beings share the same source of awakening (*bodhi*). Although delusion and enlightenment differ, their principle is eternally equal.
